arXiv:1901.02324v2 [stat.ML] 02 Mar 2020

Mathieu Blondel, André F.T. Martins, Vlad Niculae

Learning with Fenchel-Young Losses

Mathieu Blondel mathieu@mblondel.org Affiliation: NTT Communication Science Laboratories Affiliation: Kyoto, Japan    André F. T. Martins andre.martins@unbabel.com Affiliation: Unbabel & Instituto de Telecomunicações Affiliation: Lisbon, Portugal    Vlad Niculae vlad@vene.ro Affiliation: Instituto de Telecomunicações Affiliation: Lisbon, Portugal
Abstract

Over the past decades, numerous loss functions have been been proposed for a variety of supervised learning tasks, including regression, classification, ranking, and more generally structured prediction. Understanding the core principles and theoretical properties underpinning these losses is key to choose the right loss for the right problem, as well as to create new losses which combine their strengths. In this paper, we introduce Fenchel-Young losses, a generic way to construct a convex loss function for a regularized prediction function. We provide an in-depth study of their properties in a very broad setting, covering all the aforementioned supervised learning tasks, and revealing new connections between sparsity, generalized entropies, and separation margins. We show that Fenchel-Young losses unify many well-known loss functions and allow to create useful new ones easily. Finally, we derive efficient predictive and training algorithms, making Fenchel-Young losses appealing both in theory and practice.

††shortheadings: Learning with Fenchel-Young Losses / Blondel, Martins, and Niculae††firstpage: 1††heading: 21 2020 1- 1/19; Revised 10/19 1/20 19-021††editor: Sathiya Keerthi
keywords
loss functions, output regularization, convex duality, structured prediction

1 Introduction

Loss functions are a cornerstone of statistics and machine learning: They measure the difference, or “loss,” between a ground truth and a prediction. As such, much work has been devoted to designing loss functions for a variety of supervised learning tasks, including regression (Huber, 1964), classification (Crammer and Singer, 2001), ranking (Joachims, 2002) and structured prediction (Lafferty et al., 2001; Collins, 2002; Tsochantaridis et al., 2005), to name only a few well-known directions.

For the case of probabilistic classification, proper composite loss functions  (Reid and Williamson, 2010; Williamson et al., 2016) offer a principled framework unifying various existing loss functions. A proper composite loss is the composition of a proper loss between two probability distributions, with an invertible mapping from real vectors to probability distributions. The theoretical properties of proper loss functions, also known as proper scoring rules (Grünwald and Dawid (2004); Gneiting and Raftery (2007); and references therein), such as their Fisher consistency (classification calibration) and correspondence with Bregman divergences, are now well-understood. However, not all existing losses are proper composite loss functions; a notable example is the hinge loss used in support vector machines. In fact, we shall see that any loss function enjoying a separation margin, a prevalent concept in statistical learning theory which has been used to prove the famous perceptron mistake bound (Rosenblatt, 1958) and many other generalization bounds (Vapnik, 1998; Schölkopf and Smola, 2002), cannot be written in composite proper loss form.

At the same time, loss functions are often intimately related to an underlying statistical model and prediction function. For instance, the logistic loss corresponds to the multinomial distribution and the softmax operator, while the conditional random field (CRF) loss (Lafferty et al., 2001) for structured prediction is tied with marginal inference (Wainwright and Jordan, 2008). Both are instances of generalized linear models (Nelder and Baker, 1972; McCullagh and Nelder, 1989), associated with exponential family distributions. More recently, Martins and Astudillo (2016) proposed a new classification loss based on the projection onto the simplex. Unlike the logistic loss, this “sparsemax” loss induces probability distributions with sparse support, which is desirable in some applications for interpretability or computational efficiency reasons. However, the sparsemax loss was derived in a relatively ad-hoc manner and it is still relatively poorly understood. Is it one of a kind or can we generalize it in a principled manner? Thorough understanding of the core principles underpinning existing losses and their associated predictive model, potentially enabling the creation of useful new losses, is one of the main quests of this paper.

This paper.

The starting point of this paper are the notions of output regularization and regularized prediction functions, which we use to provide a variational perspective on many existing prediction functions, including the aforementioned softmax, sparsemax and marginal inference. Based on simple convex duality arguments, we then introduce Fenchel-Young losses, a new way to automatically construct a loss function associated with any regularized prediction function. As we shall see, our proposal recovers many existing loss functions, which is in a sense surprising since many of these losses were originally proposed by independent efforts. Our framework goes beyond the simple probabilistic classification setting: We show how to create loss functions over various structured domains, including convex polytopes and convex cones. Our framework encourages the loss designer to think geometrically about the outputs desired for the task at hand. Once a (regularized) prediction function has been designed, our framework generates a corresponding loss function automatically. We will demonstrate the ease of creating loss functions, including useful new ones, using abundant examples throughout this paper.

Previous papers.

This paper builds upon two previously published shorter conference papers. The first (Niculae et al., 2018) introduced Fenchel-Young losses in the structured prediction setting but only provided a limited analysis of their properties. The second (Blondel et al., 2019) provided a more in-depth analysis but focused on unstructured probabilistic classification. This paper provides a comprehensive study of Fenchel-Young losses across various domains. Besides a much more thorough treatment of previously covered topics, this paper contributes entirely new sections, including §6 on losses for positive measures, §8 on primal and dual training algorithms, and §A.2 on loss “Fenchel-Youngization”. We provide in §7 a new unifying view between structured predictions losses, and discuss at length various convex polytopes, promoting a geometric approach to structured prediction loss design; we also provide novel results in this section regarding structured separation margins (Proposition 13), proving the unit margin of the SparseMAP loss. We demonstrate how to use our framework to create useful new losses, including ranking losses, not covered in the previous two papers.

2 Regularized prediction functions

In this section, we introduce the concept of regularized prediction function (§2.1), which is central to this paper. We then give simple and well-known examples of such functions (§2.2) and discuss their properties in a general setting (§2.3,§2.4).

2.1 Definition

We consider a general predictive setting with input variables 𝒙∈𝒳{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}}, and a parametrized model 𝒇W:𝒳→ℝd\bm{f}_{W}:{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}^{d} (which could be a linear model or a neural network), producing a score vector 𝜽≔𝒇W​(𝒙)∈ℝd\bm{\theta}\coloneqq\bm{f}_{W}({\bm{x}})\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}. In a simple multi-class classification setting, the score vector is typically used to pick the highest-scoring class among dd possible ones

y^​(𝜽)∈𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑j∈[d]θj.\widehat{y}(\bm{\theta})\in\argmax_{j\in[d]}\theta_{j}. (3)

This can be generalized to an arbitrary output space 𝒴⊆ℝd{\mathcal{Y}}\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}^{d} by using instead

𝒚^​(𝜽)∈𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑𝐲∈𝒴⟨𝜽,𝐲⟩,\widehat{{\bm{y}}}(\bm{\theta})\in\argmax_{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}{{\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{y}}\rangle}}, (4)

where intuitively ⟨𝜽,𝒚⟩{\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{y}}\rangle} captures the affinity between 𝒙{\bm{x}} (since 𝜽\bm{\theta} is produced by fW​(𝒙)f_{W}({\bm{x}})) and 𝒚{\bm{y}}. Therefore, (4) seeks the output 𝒚{\bm{y}} with greatest affinity with 𝒙{\bm{x}}. The support function σ𝒴​(𝜽)=max𝒚∈𝒴⁡⟨𝜽,𝒚⟩=⟨𝜽,𝒚^​(𝜽)⟩\sigma_{\mathcal{Y}}(\bm{\theta})=\max_{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}{{\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{y}}\rangle}}={\langle\bm{\theta},\widehat{{\bm{y}}}(\bm{\theta})\rangle} can be interpreted as the largest projection of any element of 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}} onto the line generated by 𝜽\bm{\theta}.

Clearly, (4) recovers (3) with 𝒴={𝒆1,…,𝒆d}{\mathcal{Y}}=\{\bm{e}_{1},\dots,\bm{e}_{d}\}, where 𝒆j\bm{e}_{j} is a standard basis vector, 𝒆j≔[0,…​0,1⏟j,0,…​0]\bm{e}_{j}\coloneqq[0,\dots 0,\underbrace{1}_{j},0,\dots 0]. In this case, the cardinality |𝒴|{|{\mathcal{Y}}|} and the dimensionality dd coincide, but this need not be the case in general. Eq. (4) is often called a linear maximization oracle or maximum a-posteriori (MAP) oracle (Wainwright and Jordan, 2008). The latter name comes from the fact that (4) coincides with the mode of the Gibbs distribution defined by

p⁡(𝒚,𝜽)∝exp⁡⟨𝜽,𝒚⟩.p({\bm{y}};\bm{\theta})\propto\exp{\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{y}}\rangle}. (5)

Prediction over convex hulls.

We now extend the prediction function (4) by replacing 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}} with its convex hull 𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)≔{𝔼𝐩​[Y]:𝐩∈△|𝒴|}\conv({\mathcal{Y}})\coloneqq\{{\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[Y]\colon{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{|{\mathcal{Y}}|}\} and introducing a regularization function Ω\Omega into the optimization problem:

𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)∈𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑𝝁∈𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)⟨𝜽,𝝁⟩−Ω⁡(𝝁).\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})\in\argmax_{\bm{\mu}\in\conv({\mathcal{Y}})}{{\langle\bm{\theta},\bm{\mu}\rangle}}-\Omega(\bm{\mu}). (6)

We emphasize that the regularization is w.r.t. predictions (outputs) and not w.r.t. model parameters (denoted by WW in this paper), as is usually the case in the literature. We illustrate the regularized prediction function pipeline in Figure 1.

Unsurprisingly, the choice Ω=0\Omega=0 recovers the unregularized prediction function (4). This follows from the fundamental theorem of linear programming (Dantzig et al., 1955, Theorem 6), which states that the maximum of a linear form over a convex polytope is always achieved at one of its vertices:

𝒚^0​(𝜽)∈𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑𝝁∈𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)⟨𝜽,𝝁⟩=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑𝐲∈𝒴⟨𝜽,𝐲⟩.\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{0}(\bm{\theta})\in\argmax_{\bm{\mu}\in\conv({\mathcal{Y}})}{\langle\bm{\theta},\bm{\mu}\rangle}=\argmax_{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}{\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{y}}\rangle}. (7)

Why regularize outputs?

The regularized prediction function (8) casts computing a prediction as a variational problem. It involves an optimization problem that balances between two terms: an “affinity” term ⟨𝜽,𝝁⟩{\langle\bm{\theta},\bm{\mu}\rangle}, and a “confidence” term Ω⁡(𝝁)\Omega(\bm{\mu}) which should be low if 𝝁\bm{\mu} is “uncertain.” Two important classes of convex Ω\Omega are (squared) norms and, when 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)\dom(\Omega) is the probability simplex, generalized negative entropies. However, our framework does not require Ω\Omega to be convex in general.

Introducing Ω⁡(𝝁)\Omega(\bm{\mu}) in (8) tends to move the prediction away from the vertices of 𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)\conv({\mathcal{Y}}). Unless the regularization term Ω⁡(𝝁)\Omega(\bm{\mu}) is negligible compared to the affinity term ⟨𝜽,𝝁⟩{\langle\bm{\theta},\bm{\mu}\rangle}, a prediction becomes a convex combination of several vertices. As we shall see in §7, which is dedicated to structured prediction over convex hulls, we can interpret this prediction as the mean under some underlying distribution. This contrasts with (4), which always outputs the most likely vertex, i.e., the mode.

Prediction over arbitrary domains.

Regularized prediction functions are in fact not limited to convex hulls. We now state their precise definition in complete generality.

Definition 1.

Prediction function regularized by Ω\Omega

Let Ω:ℝd→ℝ∪{∞}\Omega\colon{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\to{\mathbb{R}}\cup\{\infty\} be a regularization function, with 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)⊆ℝd\dom(\Omega)\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}^{d}. The prediction function regularized by Ω\Omega is defined by

𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)∈𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑𝝁∈𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)⟨𝜽,𝝁⟩−Ω⁡(𝝁).\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})\in\argmax_{\bm{\mu}\in\dom(\Omega)}{{\langle\bm{\theta},\bm{\mu}\rangle}}-\Omega(\bm{\mu}). (8)

Allowing extended-real Ω\Omega permits general domain constraints in (8) via indicator functions. For instance, choosing Ω=I𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)\Omega=I_{\conv({\mathcal{Y}})}, where I𝒞I_{\mathcal{C}} is the indicator function defined in (1), recovers the MAP oracle (4). Importantly, the choice of domain 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)\dom(\Omega) is not limited to convex hulls. For instance, we will also consider conic hulls, 𝖼𝗈𝗇𝖾(𝒴)\cone({\mathcal{Y}}), later in this paper.

Choosing 𝛀\mathbf{\Omega}.

Regularized prediction functions 𝒚^Ω\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega} involve two main design choices: the domain 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)\dom(\Omega) over which Ω\Omega is defined and Ω\Omega itself. The choice of 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)\dom(\Omega) is mainly dictated by the type of output we want from 𝒚^Ω\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}, such as 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)=𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)\dom(\Omega)=\conv({\mathcal{Y}}) for convex combinations of elements of 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}}, and 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)=𝖼𝗈𝗇𝖾(𝒴)\dom(\Omega)=\cone({\mathcal{Y}}) for conic combinations. The choice of the regularization Ω\Omega itself further governs certain properties of 𝒚^Ω\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}, including, as we shall see in the sequel, its sparsity or its use of prior knowledge regarding the importance or misclassification cost of certain outputs. The choices of 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)\dom(\Omega) and Ω\Omega may also be constrained by computational considerations. Indeed, while computing 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) involves a potentially challenging constrained maximization problem in general, we will see that certain choices of Ω\Omega lead to closed-form expressions. The power of our framework is that the user can focus solely on designing and computing 𝒚^Ω\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}: We will see in §3 how to automatically construct a loss function associated with 𝒚^Ω\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}.

2.2 Examples

To illustrate regularized prediction functions, we give several concrete examples enjoying a closed-form expression.

When Ω=I△d\Omega=I_{\triangle^{d}}, 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) is a one-hot representation of the argmax prediction

𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)∈𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑𝐩∈△d⟨𝜽,𝐩⟩=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑𝐲∈{𝐞1,…,𝐞d}⟨𝜽,𝐲⟩.\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})\in\argmax_{{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d}}~\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{p}}\rangle=\argmax_{{\bm{y}}\in\{\bm{e}_{1},\dots,\bm{e}_{d}\}}\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{y}}\rangle. (9)

We can see that output as a probability distribution that assigns all probability mass on the same class. When Ω=−𝖧s+I△d\Omega=-\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{s}}+I_{\triangle^{d}}, where 𝖧s(𝒑)≔−∑ipilogpi\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{s}}({\bm{p}})\coloneqq-\sum_{i}p_{i}\log p_{i} is Shannon’s entropy, 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) is the well-known softmax

𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)=𝗌𝗈𝖿𝗍𝗆𝖺𝗑(𝜽)≔exp⁡(𝜽)∑j=1dexp⁡(θj).\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})=\softmax(\bm{\theta})\coloneqq\frac{\exp(\bm{\theta})}{\sum_{j=1}^{d}\exp(\theta_{j})}. (10)

See Boyd and Vandenberghe (2004, Ex. 3.25) for a derivation. The resulting distribution always has dense support. When Ω=12∥⋅∥2+I△d\Omega=\frac{1}{2}\|\cdot\|^{2}+I_{\triangle^{d}}, 𝒚^Ω\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega} is the Euclidean projection onto the probability simplex

𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)=𝗌𝗉𝖺𝗋𝗌𝖾𝗆𝖺𝗑(𝜽)≔𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝗂𝗇𝐩∈△d‖𝐩−𝜽‖2,\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})=\sparsemax(\bm{\theta})\coloneqq\argmin_{{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d}}\|{\bm{p}}-\bm{\theta}\|^{2}, (11)

a.k.a. the sparsemax transformation (Martins and Astudillo, 2016). It is well-known that

𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝗂𝗇𝐩∈△d‖𝐩−𝜽‖2=[𝜽−τ​𝟏]+,\argmin_{{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d}}\|{\bm{p}}-\bm{\theta}\|^{2}=[\bm{\theta}-\tau\bm{1}]_{+}, (12)

for some threshold τ∈ℝ\tau\in{\mathbb{R}}. Hence, the predicted distribution can have sparse support (it may assign exactly zero probability to low-scoring classes). The threshold τ\tau can be computed exactly in O⁡(d)O(d) time (Brucker, 1984; Duchi et al., 2008; Condat, 2016).

The regularized prediction function paradigm is, however, not limited to the probability simplex: When Ω(𝒑)=−∑i𝖧s([pi,1−pi])+I[0,1]d(𝒑)\Omega({\bm{p}})=-\sum_{i}\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{s}}([p_{i},1-p_{i}])+I_{[0,1]^{d}}({\bm{p}}), we get

𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)=𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗆𝗈𝗂𝖽(𝜽)≔𝟏𝟏+exp⁡(−𝜽),\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})=\sigmoid(\bm{\theta})\coloneqq\frac{\bm{1}}{\bm{1}+\exp(-\bm{\theta})}, (13)

i.e., the sigmoid function evaluated coordinate-wise. We can think of its output as a positive measure (unnormalized probability distribution).

We will see in §4 that the first three examples (argmax, softmax and sparsemax) are particular instances of a broader family of prediction functions, using the notion of generalized entropy. The last example is a special case of regularized prediction function over positive measures, developed in §6. Regularized prediction functions also encompass more complex convex polytopes for structured prediction, as we shall see in §7.

2.3 Gradient mapping and dual objective

From Danskin’s theorem (Danskin, 1966) (see also Bertsekas (1999, Proposition B.25)) 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) is a subgradient of Ω∗\Omega^{*} at 𝜽\bm{\theta}, i.e., 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)∈∂Ω∗​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})\in\partial\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta}). If, furthermore, Ω\Omega is strictly convex, then 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) is the gradient of Ω∗\Omega^{*} at 𝜽\bm{\theta}, i.e., 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)=∇Ω∗​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})=\nabla\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta}). This interpretation of 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) as a (sub)gradient mapping will play a crucial role in the next section for deriving a loss function associated with 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}).

Viewing 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) as the (sub)gradient of Ω∗​(𝜽)\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta}) is also useful to derive the dual of (8). Let Ω≔Ψ+Φ\Omega\coloneqq\Psi+\Phi. It is well-known (Borwein and Lewis, 2010; Beck and Teboulle, 2012) that

Ω∗​(𝜽)=(Ψ+Φ)∗​(𝜽)=inf𝒖∈ℝdΦ∗​(𝒖)+Ψ∗​(𝜽−𝒖)≕(Φ∗​□​Ψ∗)​(𝜽),\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta})=(\Psi+\Phi)^{*}(\bm{\theta})=\inf_{\bm{u}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\Phi^{*}(\bm{u})+\Psi^{*}(\bm{\theta}-\bm{u})\eqqcolon(\Phi^{*}\square\Psi^{*})(\bm{\theta}), (14)

where f​□​gf\square g denotes the infimal convolution of ff with gg. Furthermore, from Danskin’s theorem, 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)=∇Ψ∗​(𝜽−𝒖⋆)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})=\nabla\Psi^{*}(\bm{\theta}-\bm{u}^{\star}), where 𝒖⋆\bm{u}^{\star} denotes an optimal solution of the infimum in (14). We can think of that infimum as the dual of the optimization problem in (8). When Ψ=Ψ∗=12∥⋅∥2\Psi=\Psi^{*}=\frac{1}{2}\|\cdot\|^{2}, Ω∗​(𝜽)\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta}) is known as the Moreau envelope of Φ∗\Phi^{*} (Moreau, 1965) and using Moreau’s decomposition, we obtain 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)=𝜽−𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑Φ∗​(𝜽)=𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑Φ​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})=\bm{\theta}-\mathsf{prox}_{\Phi^{*}}(\bm{\theta})=\mathsf{prox}_{\Phi}(\bm{\theta}). As another example, when Ω=Ψ+I𝒞\Omega=\Psi+I_{\mathcal{C}}, we obtain

Ω∗​(𝜽)=inf𝒖∈ℝdσ𝒞​(𝒖)+Ψ∗​(𝜽−𝒖),\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta})=\inf_{\bm{u}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\sigma_{\mathcal{C}}(\bm{u})+\Psi^{*}(\bm{\theta}-\bm{u}), (15)

where we used I𝒞∗=σ𝒞I_{\mathcal{C}}^{*}=\sigma_{\mathcal{C}}, the support function of 𝒞{\mathcal{C}}. In particular, when 𝒞=𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴){\mathcal{C}}=\conv({\mathcal{Y}}), we have σ𝒞​(𝒖)=max𝒚∈𝒴⁡⟨𝒖,𝒚⟩\sigma_{\mathcal{C}}(\bm{u})=\max_{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}{\langle\bm{u},{\bm{y}}\rangle}. This dual view is informative insofar as it suggests that regularized prediction functions 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) with Ω=Ψ+I𝒞\Omega=\Psi+I_{\mathcal{C}} minimize a trade-off between maximizing the value achieved by the unregularized prediction function σ𝒞​(𝒖)\sigma_{\mathcal{C}}(\bm{u}), and a proximity term Ψ∗​(𝜽−𝒖)\Psi^{*}(\bm{\theta}-\bm{u}).

2.4 Properties

We now discuss simple yet useful properties of regularized prediction functions. The first two assume that Ω\Omega is a symmetric function, i.e., that it satisfies

Ω⁡(𝝁)=Ω⁡(𝑷​𝝁)∀𝝁∈𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω),∀𝐏∈𝒫,\Omega(\bm{\mu})=\Omega(\bm{P}\bm{\mu})\quad\forall\bm{\mu}\in\dom(\Omega),\forall\bm{P}\in\mathcal{P}, (16)

where 𝒫\mathcal{P} is the set of d×dd\times d permutation matrices.

Proposition 2.

Properties of regularized prediction functions 𝐲^Ω​(𝛉)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})

  1. 1.

    Effect of a permutation. If Ω\Omega is symmetric, then ∀𝑷∈𝒫\forall\bm{P}\in\mathcal{P}: 𝒚^Ω​(𝑷​𝜽)=𝑷​𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{P}\bm{\theta})=\bm{P}\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}).

  2. 2.

    Order preservation. Let 𝝁=𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\bm{\mu}=\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}). If Ω\Omega is symmetric, then the coordinates of 𝝁\bm{\mu} and 𝜽\bm{\theta} are sorted the same way, i.e., θi>θj⇒μi≥μj\theta_{i}>\theta_{j}\Rightarrow\mu_{i}\geq\mu_{j} and μi>μj⇒θi>θj\mu_{i}>\mu_{j}\Rightarrow\theta_{i}>\theta_{j}.

  3. 3.

    Approximation error. Assume 𝒴⊆𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)\mathcal{Y}\subseteq\dom(\Omega). If Ω\Omega is γ\gamma-strongly convex and bounded with L≤Ω⁡(𝝁)≤UL\leq\Omega(\bm{\mu})\leq U for all 𝝁∈𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)\bm{\mu}\in\dom(\Omega), then 12​‖𝒚^​(𝜽)−𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)‖2≤U−Lγ\frac{1}{2}\|\widehat{{\bm{y}}}(\bm{\theta})-\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})\|^{2}\leq\frac{U-L}{\gamma}.

  4. 4.

    Temperature scaling. For any constant t>0t>0, 𝒚^t​Ω​(𝜽)∈∂Ω∗​(𝜽/t)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{t\Omega}(\bm{\theta})\in\partial\Omega^{*}(\nicefrac{{\bm{\theta}}}{{t}}). If Ω\Omega is strictly convex, 𝒚^t​Ω​(𝜽)=𝒚^Ω​(𝜽/t)=∇Ω∗​(𝜽/t)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{t\Omega}(\bm{\theta})=\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\nicefrac{{\bm{\theta}}}{{t}})=\nabla\Omega^{*}(\nicefrac{{\bm{\theta}}}{{t}}).

  5. 5.

    Constant invariance. For any constant c∈ℝc\in{\mathbb{R}}, 𝒚^Ω+c​(𝜽)=𝒚^Ω​(𝜽,𝒚)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega+c}(\bm{\theta})=\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}}).

The proof is given in Appendix B.1.

For classification, the order-preservation property ensures that the highest-scoring class according to 𝜽\bm{\theta} and 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) agree with each other:

𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑i∈[d]θi=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑i∈[d](𝐲^Ω​(𝜽))i.\argmax_{i\in[d]}\theta_{i}=\argmax_{i\in[d]}\left(\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})\right)_{i}. (17)

Temperature scaling is useful to control how close we are to unregularized prediction functions. Clearly, 𝒚^t​Ω​(𝜽)→𝒚^​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{t\Omega}(\bm{\theta})\to\widehat{{\bm{y}}}(\bm{\theta}) as t→0t\to 0, where 𝒚^​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}(\bm{\theta}) is defined in (4).

3 Fenchel-Young losses

In the previous section, we introduced regularized prediction functions over arbitrary domains, as a generalization of classical (unregularized) decision functions. In this section, we introduce Fenchel-Young losses for learning models whose output layer is a regularized prediction function. We first give their definitions and state their properties (§3.1). We then discuss their relationship with Bregman divergences (§3.2) and their Bayes risk (§3.3). Finally, we show how to construct a cost-sensitive loss from any Fenchel-Young loss (§3.4).

3.1 Definition and properties

Given a regularized prediction function 𝒚^Ω\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}, we define its associated loss as follows.

Definition 3.

Fenchel-Young loss generated by Ω\Omega

Let Ω:ℝd→ℝ∪{∞}\Omega\colon{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\to{\mathbb{R}}\cup\{\infty\} be a regularization function such that the maximum in (8) is achieved for all 𝛉∈ℝd\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}. Let 𝐲∈𝒴⊆𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω){\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}\subseteq\dom(\Omega) be a ground-truth label and 𝛉∈𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω∗)=ℝd\bm{\theta}\in\dom(\Omega^{*})={\mathbb{R}}^{d} be a vector of prediction scores.

The Fenchel-Young loss LΩ:𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω∗)×𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)→ℝ+L_{\Omega}\colon\dom(\Omega^{*})\times\dom(\Omega)\to{\mathbb{R}}_{+} generated by Ω\Omega is

LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)≔Ω∗​(𝜽)+Ω⁡(𝒚)−⟨𝜽,𝒚⟩.L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})\coloneqq\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta})+\Omega({\bm{y}})-{\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{y}}\rangle}. (18)

It is easy to see that Fenchel-Young losses can be rewritten as

LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)=f𝜽​(𝒚)−f𝜽​(𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)),L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=f_{\bm{\theta}}({\bm{y}})-f_{\bm{\theta}}(\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})), (19)

where f𝜽​(𝝁)≔Ω⁡(𝝁)−⟨𝜽,𝝁⟩f_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\mu})\coloneqq\Omega(\bm{\mu})-{\langle\bm{\theta},\bm{\mu}\rangle}, highlighting the relation with regularized prediction functions. Therefore, as long as we can compute a regularized prediction function 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}), we can automatically obtain an associated Fenchel-Young loss LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}}). Conversely, we also have that 𝒚^Ω\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega} outputs the prediction minimizing the loss:

𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)∈𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝗂𝗇𝝁∈𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)LΩ​(𝜽,𝝁).\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})\in\argmin_{\bm{\mu}\in\dom(\Omega)}L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};\bm{\mu}). (20)

Examples of existing losses that fall into the Fenchel-Young loss family are given in Table 1. Some of these examples will be discussed in more details in the sequel of this paper. Note that we will allow Ω\Omega in some cases to depend on the ground-truth 𝒚{\bm{y}}. Since we do not know 𝒚{\bm{y}} at test time, this requires us to use another prediction function as a replacement for the regularized prediction function. As we explain in §3.4, this discrepancy is well motivated and allows us to express popular cost-sensitive losses, such as the structured hinge loss.

Properties.

As the name indicates, this family of loss functions is grounded in the Fenchel-Young inequality (Borwein and Lewis, 2010, Proposition 3.3.4)

Ω∗​(𝜽)+Ω⁡(𝝁)≥⟨𝜽,𝝁⟩∀𝜽∈𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω∗),𝝁∈𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω).\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta})+\Omega(\bm{\mu})\geq{\langle\bm{\theta},\bm{\mu}\rangle}\quad\forall\bm{\theta}\in\dom(\Omega^{*}),\bm{\mu}\in\dom(\Omega). (21)

The inequality, together with well-known results regarding convex conjugates, imply the following properties of Fenchel-Young losses.

Proposition 4.

Properties of Fenchel-Young losses

  1. 1.

    Non-negativity. LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)≥0L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})\geq 0 for any 𝜽∈𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω∗)=ℝd\bm{\theta}\in\dom(\Omega^{*})={\mathbb{R}}^{d} and 𝒚∈𝒴⊆𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω){\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}\subseteq\dom(\Omega).

  2. 2.

    Zero loss. If Ω\Omega is a lower semi-continuous proper convex function, then
    min𝜽⁡LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)=0\min_{\bm{\theta}}L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=0, and LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)=0⇔𝒚∈∂Ω∗​(𝜽)L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=0\Leftrightarrow{\bm{y}}\in\partial\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta}). If Ω\Omega is strictly convex, then LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)=0⇔𝒚=𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)=∇Ω∗​(𝜽)=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝗂𝗇𝜽∈ℝdLΩ​(𝜽,𝐲)L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=0\Leftrightarrow{\bm{y}}=\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})=\nabla\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta})=\argmin_{\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}}).

  3. 3.

    Convexity & subgradients. LΩL_{\Omega} is convex in 𝜽\bm{\theta} and the residual vectors are its subgradients: 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)−𝒚∈∂LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})-{\bm{y}}\in\partial L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}}).

  4. 4.

    Differentiability & smoothness. If Ω\Omega is strictly convex, then LΩL_{\Omega} is differentiable and ∇LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)=𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)−𝒚\nabla L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})-{\bm{y}}. If Ω\Omega is strongly convex, then LΩL_{\Omega} is smooth, i.e., ∇LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)\nabla L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}}) is Lipschitz continuous.

  5. 5.

    Temperature scaling. For any constant t>0t>0, Lt​Ω​(𝜽,𝒚)=t​LΩ​(𝜽/t,𝒚)L_{t\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=tL_{\Omega}(\nicefrac{{\bm{\theta}}}{{t}};{\bm{y}}).

  6. 6.

    Constant invariance. For any constant c∈ℝc\in{\mathbb{R}}, LΩ+c​(𝜽,𝒚)=LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)L_{\Omega+c}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}}).

Remarkably, the non-negativity, convexity and constant invariance properties hold even if Ω\Omega is not convex. The zero loss property follows from the fact that, if Ω\Omega is l.s.c. proper convex, then (21) becomes an equality (i.e., the duality gap is zero) if and only if 𝜽∈∂Ω⁡(𝝁)\bm{\theta}\in\partial\Omega(\bm{\mu}). It suggests that the minimization of Fenchel-Young losses attempts to adjust the model to produce predictions 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) that are close to the target 𝒚{\bm{y}}, reducing the duality gap. This is illustrated with Ω=12​‖𝝁‖2\Omega=\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{\mu}\|^{2} and 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)=ℝd\dom(\Omega)={\mathbb{R}}^{d} (leading to the squared loss) in Figure 3.

Domain of 𝛀∗\mathbf{\Omega^{*}}.

Our assumption that the maximum in the regularized prediction function (8) is achieved for all 𝜽∈ℝd\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} implies that 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω∗)=ℝd\dom(\Omega^{*})={\mathbb{R}}^{d}. This assumption is quite mild and does not require 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)\dom(\Omega) to be bounded. Minimizing LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}}) w.r.t. 𝜽\bm{\theta} is therefore an unconstrained convex optimization problem. This contrasts with proper loss functions, which are defined over the probability simplex, as discussed in §10.

3.2 Relation with Bregman divergences

Fenchel-Young losses seamlessly work when 𝒴=𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω){\mathcal{Y}}=\dom(\Omega) instead of 𝒴⊂𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω){\mathcal{Y}}\subset\dom(\Omega). For example, in the case of the logistic loss, where −Ω-\Omega is the Shannon entropy restricted to △d\triangle^{d}, allowing 𝒚∈△d{\bm{y}}\in\triangle^{d} instead of 𝒚∈{𝒆i}i=1d{\bm{y}}\in\{\bm{e}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{d} yields the cross-entropy loss, LΩ(𝜽;𝒚)=𝖪𝖫(𝒚∥𝗌𝗈𝖿𝗍𝗆𝖺𝗑(𝜽))L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=\mathsf{KL}({\bm{y}}\|\softmax(\bm{\theta})), where 𝖪𝖫\mathsf{KL} denotes the (generalized) Kullback-Leibler divergence

𝖪𝖫(𝒚∥𝝁)≔∑iyilogyiμi−∑iyi+∑iμi.\mathsf{KL}({\bm{y}}\|\bm{\mu})\coloneqq\sum_{i}y_{i}\log\frac{y_{i}}{\mu_{i}}-\sum_{i}y_{i}+\sum_{i}\mu_{i}. (22)

This can be useful in a multi-label setting with supervision in the form of label proportions.

From this example, it is tempting to conjecture that a similar result holds for more general Bregman divergences (Bregman, 1967). Recall that the Bregman divergence BΩ:𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)×𝗋𝖾𝗅𝗂𝗇𝗍(𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω))→ℝ+B_{\Omega}\colon\dom(\Omega)\times\relint(\dom(\Omega))\to{\mathbb{R}}_{+} generated by a strictly convex and differentiable Ω\Omega is

BΩ(𝒚∥𝝁)≔Ω(𝒚)−Ω(𝝁)−⟨∇Ω(𝝁),𝒚−𝝁⟩.B_{\Omega}({\bm{y}}\|\bm{\mu})\coloneqq\Omega({\bm{y}})-\Omega(\bm{\mu})-{\langle\nabla\Omega(\bm{\mu}),{\bm{y}}-\bm{\mu}\rangle}. (23)

In other words, this is the difference at 𝒚{\bm{y}} between Ω\Omega and its linearization around 𝝁\bm{\mu}. It turns out that LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}}) is not in general equal to BΩ(𝒚∥𝒚^Ω(𝜽))B_{\Omega}({\bm{y}}\|\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})). In fact the latter is not necessarily convex in 𝜽\bm{\theta} while the former always is. However, there is a duality relationship between Fenchel-Young losses and Bregman divergences, as we now discuss.

A “mixed-space” Bregman divergence.

Letting 𝜽=∇Ω​(𝝁)\bm{\theta}=\nabla\Omega(\bm{\mu}) (i.e., (𝜽,𝝁)(\bm{\theta},\bm{\mu}) is a dual pair), we have Ω∗​(𝜽)=⟨𝜽,𝝁⟩−Ω⁡(𝝁)\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta})={\langle\bm{\theta},\bm{\mu}\rangle}-\Omega(\bm{\mu}). Substituting in (23), we get BΩ(𝒚∥𝝁)=LΩ(𝜽;𝒚).B_{\Omega}({\bm{y}}\|\bm{\mu})=L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}}). In other words, Fenchel-Young losses can be viewed as a “mixed-form Bregman divergence” (Amari, 2016, Theorem 1.1) where the argument 𝝁\bm{\mu} in (23) is replaced by its dual point 𝜽\bm{\theta}. This difference is best seen by comparing the function signatures, LΩ:𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω∗)×𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)→ℝ+L_{\Omega}\colon\dom(\Omega^{*})\times\dom(\Omega)\to{\mathbb{R}}_{+} vs. BΩ:𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)×𝗋𝖾𝗅𝗂𝗇𝗍(𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω))→ℝ+B_{\Omega}\colon\dom(\Omega)\times\relint(\dom(\Omega))\to{\mathbb{R}}_{+}. An important consequence is that Fenchel-Young losses do not impose any restriction on their left argument 𝜽\bm{\theta}: Our assumption that the maximum in the prediction function (8) is achieved for all 𝜽∈ℝd\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} implies 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω∗)=ℝd\dom(\Omega^{*})={\mathbb{R}}^{d}. In contrast, a Bregman divergence would typically need to be composed with a mapping from ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{d} to 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)\dom(\Omega), such as 𝒚^Ω\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}, resulting in a possibly non-convex function.

Case of Legendre-type functions.

We can make the relationship with Bregman divergences further precise when Ω=Ψ+I𝒞\Omega=\Psi+I_{\mathcal{C}}, where Ψ\Psi is restricted to the class of so-called Legendre-type functions (Rockafellar, 1970; Wainwright and Jordan, 2008). We first recall the definition of this class of functions and then state our results.

Definition 5.

Essentially smooth and Legendre type functions

A function Ψ\Psi is essentially smooth if

  • •

    𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ψ)\dom(\Psi) is non-empty,

  • •

    Ψ\Psi is differentiable throughout 𝗂𝗇𝗍(𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ψ))\interior(\dom(\Psi)),

  • •

    and limi→∞∇Ψ​(𝝁i)=+∞\lim_{i\to\infty}\nabla\Psi(\bm{\mu}^{i})=+\infty for any sequence {𝝁i}\{\bm{\mu}^{i}\} contained in 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ψ)\dom(\Psi), and converging to a boundary point of 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ψ)\dom(\Psi).

A function Ψ\Psi is of Legendre type if

  • •

    it is strictly convex on 𝗂𝗇𝗍(𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ψ))\interior(\dom(\Psi))

  • •

    and essentially smooth.

For instance, Ψ⁡(𝝁)=12​‖𝝁‖2\Psi(\bm{\mu})=\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{\mu}\|^{2} is Legendre-type with 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ψ)=ℝd\dom(\Psi)={\mathbb{R}}^{d}, and Ψ⁡(𝝁)=∑iμi​log⁡μi\Psi(\bm{\mu})=\sum_{i}\mu_{i}\log\mu_{i} is Legendre-type with 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ψ)=ℝ+d\dom(\Psi)={\mathbb{R}}^{d}_{+}. However, Ω⁡(𝝁)=12​‖𝝁‖2+Iℝ+d​(𝝁)\Omega(\bm{\mu})=\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{\mu}\|^{2}+I_{{\mathbb{R}}_{+}^{d}}(\bm{\mu}) is not Legendre-type, since the gradient of Ω\Omega does not explode everywhere on the boundary of ℝ+d{\mathbb{R}}_{+}^{d}. The Legendre-type assumption crucially implies that

∇Ψ​(∇Ψ∗​(𝜽))=𝜽for all𝜽∈𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ψ∗).\nabla\Psi(\nabla\Psi^{*}(\bm{\theta}))=\bm{\theta}\quad\text{for all}\quad\bm{\theta}\in\dom(\Psi^{*}). (24)

We can use this fact to derive the following results, proved in Appendix B.2.

Proposition 6.

Relation with Bregman divergences

Let Ψ\Psi be of Legendre type with 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ψ∗)=ℝd\dom(\Psi^{*})={\mathbb{R}}^{d} and let 𝒞⊆𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ψ){\mathcal{C}}\subseteq\dom(\Psi) be a convex set.
Let Ω\Omega be the restriction of Ψ\Psi to 𝒞⊆𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ψ){\mathcal{C}}\subseteq\dom(\Psi), i.e., Ω≔Ψ+I𝒞\Omega\coloneqq\Psi+I_{\mathcal{C}}.

  1. 1.

    Bregman projection. The prediction function regularized by Ω\Omega, 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}), reduces to the Bregman projection of 𝒚^Ψ​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Psi}(\bm{\theta}) onto 𝒞{\mathcal{C}}:

    𝒚^Ω(𝜽)=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑𝝁∈𝒞⟨𝜽,𝝁⟩−Ψ(𝝁)=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝗂𝗇𝝁∈𝒞BΨ(𝝁∥𝐲^Ψ(𝜽)).\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})=\argmax_{\bm{\mu}\in{\mathcal{C}}}{\langle\bm{\theta},\bm{\mu}\rangle}-\Psi(\bm{\mu})=\argmin_{\bm{\mu}\in{\mathcal{C}}}B_{\Psi}(\bm{\mu}\|\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Psi}(\bm{\theta})). (25)
  2. 2.

    Difference of divergences. For all 𝜽∈ℝd\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} and 𝒚∈𝒞{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{C}}:

    LΩ(𝜽;𝒚)=BΨ(𝒚∥𝒚^Ψ(𝜽))−BΨ(𝒚^Ω(𝜽)∥𝒚^Ψ(𝜽)).L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=B_{\Psi}({\bm{y}}\|\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Psi}(\bm{\theta}))-B_{\Psi}(\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})\|\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Psi}(\bm{\theta})). (26)
  3. 3.

    Bound. For all 𝜽∈ℝd\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} and 𝒚∈𝒞{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{C}}:

    0≤BΨ(𝒚∥𝒚^Ω(𝜽))⏟possibly non-convex in 𝜽≤LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)⏟convex in ​𝜽0\leq\underbrace{B_{\Psi}({\bm{y}}\|\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}))}_{\text{possibly non-convex in }\bm{\theta}}\leq\underbrace{L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})}_{\text{convex in }\bm{\theta}} (27)

    with equality when the loss is minimized

    𝒚^Ω(𝜽)=𝒚⇔LΩ(𝜽;𝒚)=0⇔BΨ(𝒚∥𝒚^Ω(𝜽))=0.\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})={\bm{y}}\Leftrightarrow L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=0\Leftrightarrow B_{\Psi}({\bm{y}}\|\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}))=0. (28)
  4. 4.

    Composite form. When 𝒞=𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ψ){\mathcal{C}}=\dom(\Psi), i.e., Ω=Ψ\Omega=\Psi, we have equality for all 𝜽∈ℝd\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}

    LΩ(𝜽;𝒚)=BΩ(𝒚∥𝒚^Ω(𝜽)).L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=B_{\Omega}({\bm{y}}\|\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})). (29)

We illustrate these properties using Ψ=12∥⋅∥2\Psi=\frac{1}{2}\|\cdot\|^{2} as a running example. From the first property, since 𝒚^Ψ​(𝜽)=𝜽\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Psi}(\bm{\theta})=\bm{\theta} and BΨ(𝒚∥𝝁)=12∥𝒚−𝝁∥2B_{\Psi}({\bm{y}}\|\bm{\mu})=\frac{1}{2}\|{\bm{y}}-\bm{\mu}\|^{2}, we get

𝒚^Ω(𝜽)=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝗂𝗇𝝁∈𝒞BΨ(𝝁∥𝐲^Ψ(𝜽))=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝗂𝗇𝝁∈𝒞BΨ(𝝁∥𝜽)=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝗂𝗇𝝁∈𝒞∥𝝁−𝜽∥2,\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})=\argmin_{\bm{\mu}\in{\mathcal{C}}}B_{\Psi}(\bm{\mu}\|\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Psi}(\bm{\theta}))=\argmin_{\bm{\mu}\in{\mathcal{C}}}B_{\Psi}(\bm{\mu}\|\bm{\theta})=\argmin_{\bm{\mu}\in{\mathcal{C}}}\|\bm{\mu}-\bm{\theta}\|^{2}, (30)

recovering the Euclidean projection onto 𝒞{\mathcal{C}}. The reduction of regularized prediction functions to Bregman projections (when Ψ\Psi is of Legendre type) is useful because there exist efficient algorithms for computing the Bregman projection onto various convex sets (Yasutake et al., 2011; Suehiro et al., 2012; Krichene et al., 2015; Lim and Wright, 2016). Therefore, we can use these algorithms to compute 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) provided that 𝒚^Ψ​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Psi}(\bm{\theta}) is available.

From the second property, we obtain for all 𝜽∈ℝd\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} and 𝒚∈𝒞{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{C}}

LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)=12​‖𝒚−𝜽‖2−12​‖𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)−𝜽‖2.L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=\frac{1}{2}\|{\bm{y}}-\bm{\theta}\|^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\|\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})-\bm{\theta}\|^{2}. (31)

This recovers the expression of the sparsemax loss given in Table 1 with 𝒞=△d{\mathcal{C}}=\triangle^{d}.

From the third claim, we obtain for all 𝜽∈ℝd\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} and 𝒚∈𝒞{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{C}}

12​‖𝒚−𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)‖2≤LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚).\frac{1}{2}\|{\bm{y}}-\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})\|^{2}\leq L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}}). (32)

This shows that LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}}) provides a convex upper-bound for the possibly non-convex composite function BΨ(𝒚∥𝒚^Ω(𝜽))B_{\Psi}({\bm{y}}\|\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})). In particular, when 𝒞=△d{\mathcal{C}}=\triangle^{d}, we get 12​‖𝒚−𝗌𝗉𝖺𝗋𝗌𝖾𝗆𝖺𝗑(𝜽)‖2≤LΩ​(𝜽,𝐲)\frac{1}{2}\|{\bm{y}}-\sparsemax(\bm{\theta})\|^{2}\leq L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}}). This suggests that the sparsemax loss is useful for sparse label proportion estimation, as confirmed in our experiments (§9).

Finally, from the last property, if Ω=Ψ=12∥⋅∥2\Omega=\Psi=\frac{1}{2}\|\cdot\|^{2}, we obtain LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)=12​‖𝒚−𝜽‖2L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=\frac{1}{2}\|{\bm{y}}-\bm{\theta}\|^{2}, which is indeed the squared loss given in Table 1.

3.3 Expected loss, Bayes risk and Bregman information

In this section, we discuss the relation between the pointwise Bayes risk (minimal achievable loss) of a Fenchel-Young loss and Bregman information (Banerjee et al., 2005).

Expected loss.

Let YY be a random variable taking values in 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}} following the distribution 𝒑∈△|𝒴|{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{|{\mathcal{Y}}|}. The expected loss (a.k.a. expected risk) is then

𝔼𝒑​[LΩ​(𝜽,Y)]\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};Y)] =∑𝒚∈𝒴p⁡(𝒚)​LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)\displaystyle=\sum_{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}p({\bm{y}})L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}}) (33)
=∑𝒚∈𝒴p⁡(𝒚)​(Ω∗​(𝜽)+Ω⁡(𝒚)−⟨𝜽,𝒚⟩)\displaystyle=\sum_{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}p({\bm{y}})(\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta})+\Omega({\bm{y}})-{\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{y}}\rangle}) (34)
=𝔼𝒑​[Ω⁡(Y)]+Ω∗​(𝜽)−⟨𝜽,𝔼𝒑​[Y]⟩\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[\Omega(Y)]+\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta})-{\langle\bm{\theta},{\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[Y]\rangle} (35)
=LΩ​(𝜽,𝔼𝒑​[Y])+𝕀Ω​(Y,𝒑).\displaystyle=L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[Y])+{\mathbb{I}}_{\Omega}(Y;{\bm{p}}). (36)

Here, we defined the Bregman information of YY by

𝕀Ω(Y;𝒑)≔min𝝁∈𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)𝔼𝒑[BΩ(Y∥𝝁)]=𝔼𝒑[BΩ(Y∥𝔼𝒑[Y])]=𝔼𝒑[Ω(Y)]−Ω(𝔼𝒑[Y]).{\mathbb{I}}_{\Omega}(Y;{\bm{p}})\coloneqq\min_{\bm{\mu}\in\dom(\Omega)}{\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[B_{\Omega}(Y\|\bm{\mu})]={\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}\left[B_{\Omega}(Y\|{\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[Y])\right]={\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[\Omega(Y)]-\Omega({\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[Y]). (37)

We refer the reader to Banerjee et al. (2005) for a detailed discussion as to why the last two equalities hold. The r.h.s. is exactly equal to the difference between the two sides of Jensen’s inequality 𝔼⁡[Ω⁡(Y)]≥Ω⁡(𝔼⁡[Y]){\mathbb{E}}[\Omega(Y)]\geq\Omega({\mathbb{E}}[Y]) and is therefore non-negative. For this reason, it is sometimes also called Jensen gap (Reid and Williamson, 2011).

Bayes risk.

From Proposition 4, we know that min𝜽⁡LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)=0\min_{\bm{\theta}}L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=0 for all 𝒚∈𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω){\bm{y}}\in\dom(\Omega). Therefore, the pointwise Bayes risk coincides precisely with the Bregman information of YY,

min𝜽∈ℝd⁡𝔼𝒑​[LΩ​(𝜽,Y)]=min𝜽∈ℝd⁡LΩ​(𝜽,𝔼𝒑​[Y])+𝕀Ω​(Y,𝒑)=𝕀Ω​(Y,𝒑),\min_{\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}{\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};Y)]=\min_{\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[Y])+{\mathbb{I}}_{\Omega}(Y;{\bm{p}})={\mathbb{I}}_{\Omega}(Y;{\bm{p}}), (38)

provided that 𝔼𝒑​[Y]∈𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω){\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[Y]\in\dom(\Omega). A similar relation between Bayes risk and Bregman information exists for proper losses (Reid and Williamson, 2011). We can think of (38) as a measure of the “difficulty” of the task. Combining (36) and (38), we obtain

𝔼𝒑​[LΩ​(𝜽,Y)]−min𝜽∈ℝd⁡𝔼𝒑​[LΩ​(𝜽,Y)]=LΩ​(𝜽,𝔼𝒑​[Y]),{\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};Y)]-\min_{\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}{\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};Y)]=L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[Y]), (39)

the pointwise “regret” of 𝜽∈ℝd\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} w.r.t. 𝒑∈△|𝒴|{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{|{\mathcal{Y}}|}. If 𝒴={𝒆i}i=1d{\mathcal{Y}}=\{\bm{e}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{d}, LΩ​(𝜽,𝔼𝒑​[Y])=LΩ​(𝜽,𝒑)L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[Y])=L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{p}}).

3.4 Cost-sensitive losses

Fenchel-Young losses also include the hinge loss of support vector machines. Indeed, from any classification loss LΩL_{\Omega}, we can construct a cost-sensitive version of it as follows. Define

Ψ⁡(𝝁,𝒚)≔Ω⁡(𝝁)−⟨𝒄𝒚,𝝁⟩,\Psi(\bm{\mu};{\bm{y}})\coloneqq\Omega(\bm{\mu})-{\langle\bm{c}_{{\bm{y}}},\bm{\mu}\rangle}, (40)

where 𝒄𝒚∈ℝ+|𝒴|\bm{c}_{{\bm{y}}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{|{\mathcal{Y}}|}_{+} is a fixed cost vector that may depend on the ground truth 𝒚{\bm{y}}. For example, 𝒄𝒚=𝟏−𝒚\bm{c}_{{\bm{y}}}=\mathbf{1}-{\bm{y}} corresponds to the 0/1 cost and can be used to impose a margin. Then, LΨL_{\Psi} is a cost-sensitive version of LΩL_{\Omega}, which can be written as

LΨ⁡(⋅,𝒚)​(𝜽,𝒚)=LΩ​(𝜽+𝒄𝒚,𝒚)=Ω∗​(𝜽+𝒄𝒚)+Ω⁡(𝒚)−⟨𝜽+𝒄𝒚,𝒚⟩.L_{\Psi(\cdot;{\bm{y}})}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}+\bm{c}_{\bm{y}};{\bm{y}})=\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta}+\bm{c}_{\bm{y}})+\Omega({\bm{y}})-{\langle\bm{\theta}+\bm{c}_{{\bm{y}}},{\bm{y}}\rangle}. (41)

This construction recovers the multi-class hinge loss (Crammer and Singer (2001); Ω=0\Omega=0), the softmax-margin loss (Gimpel and Smith (2010); Ω=−𝖧s\Omega=-\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{s}}), and the cost-augmented sparsemax (Shalev-Shwartz and Zhang (2016, Eq. (13)), Niculae et al. (2018); Ω=12∥⋅∥2\Omega=\frac{1}{2}\|\cdot\|^{2}). It is easy to see that the associated regularized prediction function is

𝒚^Ψ​(𝜽)=𝒚^Ω​(𝜽+𝒄𝒚).\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Psi}(\bm{\theta})=\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}+\bm{c}_{\bm{y}}). (42)

For the 0/1 cost 𝒄𝒚=𝟏−𝒚\bm{c}_{{\bm{y}}}=\mathbf{1}-{\bm{y}} and 𝒚=𝒆k{\bm{y}}=\bm{e}_{k}, we have

𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑i∈[d](𝐲^Ψ​(𝜽))i=k⟹𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑i∈[d](𝐲^Ω​(𝜽))i=k,\argmax_{i\in[d]}~(\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Psi}(\bm{\theta}))_{i}=k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\argmax_{i\in[d]}~(\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}))_{i}=k, (43)

justifying the use of 𝒚^Ω\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega} at prediction time.

4 Probabilistic prediction with Fenchel-Young losses

In the previous section, we presented Fenchel-Young losses in a broad setting. We now restrict to classification over the probability simplex. More precisely, we restrict to the case 𝒴={𝒆i}i=1d{\mathcal{Y}}=\{\bm{e}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{d}, (i.e., unstructured multi-class classification), and assume that 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)⊆𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)=△d\dom(\Omega)\subseteq\conv({\mathcal{Y}})=\triangle^{d}. In this case, the regularized prediction function (8) becomes

𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)∈𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑𝐩∈△d⟨𝜽,𝐩⟩−Ω⁡(𝐩),\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})\in\argmax_{{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d}}{{\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{p}}\rangle}}-\Omega({\bm{p}}), (44)

where 𝜽∈ℝd\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} is a vector of (possibly negative) prediction scores produced by a model 𝒇W​(𝒙)\bm{f}_{W}({\bm{x}}) and 𝒑∈△d{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d} is a discrete probability distribution. It is a generalized exponential family distribution (Grünwald and Dawid, 2004; Frongillo and Reid, 2014) with natural parameter 𝜽∈ℝd\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} and regularization Ω\Omega. Of particular interest is the case where 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) is sparse, meaning that there are scores 𝜽\bm{\theta} for which the resulting 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) assigns zero probability to some classes. As seen in §2.2, this happens for example with the sparsemax transformation, but not with the softmax. Later, in §5, we will establish conditions for the regularized prediction function to be sparse and will connect it to the notion of separation margin.

We first discuss generalized entropies and the properties of the Fenchel-Young losses they induce (§4.1). We then discuss their expected loss, Bayes risk and Fisher consistency (§4.2). We then give examples of generalized entropies and corresponding loss functions, several of them new to our knowledge (§4.3). Finally, we discuss the binary classification setting, recovering several examples of commonly-used loss functions (§4.4).

4.1 Fenchel-Young loss generated by a generalized entropy

Generalized entropies.

A natural choice of regularization function Ω\Omega over the probability simplex is Ω=−𝖧\Omega=-\mathsf{H}, where 𝖧\mathsf{H} is a generalized entropy (Grünwald and Dawid, 2004), also called uncertainty function by DeGroot (1962): a concave function over △d\triangle^{d}, used to measure the “uncertainty” in a distribution 𝒑∈△d{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d}.

Assumptions: We will make the following assumptions about 𝖧\mathsf{H}.

  1. A.1.

    Zero entropy: 𝖧⁡(𝒑)=0\mathsf{H}({\bm{p}})=0 if 𝒑{\bm{p}} is a delta distribution, i.e., 𝒑∈{𝒆i}i=1d{\bm{p}}\in\{\bm{e}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{d}.

  2. A.2.

    Strict concavity: 𝖧⁡((1−α)​𝒑+α​𝒑′)>(1−α)​𝖧​(𝒑)+α​𝖧​(𝒑′)\mathsf{H}\big((1-\alpha){\bm{p}}+\alpha{\bm{p}}^{\prime}\big)>{(1-\alpha)}\mathsf{H}({\bm{p}})+\alpha\mathsf{H}({\bm{p}}^{\prime}), for 𝒑≠𝒑′{\bm{p}}\neq{\bm{p}}^{\prime}, α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1).

  3. A.3.

    Symmetry: 𝖧⁡(𝒑)=𝖧⁡(𝑷​𝒑)\mathsf{H}({\bm{p}})=\mathsf{H}(\bm{P}{\bm{p}}) for any 𝑷∈𝒫\bm{P}\in\mathcal{P}.

Assumptions A.2 and A.3 imply that 𝖧\mathsf{H} is Schur-concave (Bauschke and Combettes, 2017), a common requirement in generalized entropies. This in turn implies assumption A.1, up to a constant (that constant can easily be subtracted so as to satisfy assumption A.1). As suggested by the next result, proved in §B.3, together, these assumptions imply that 𝖧\mathsf{H} can be used as a sensible uncertainty measure.

Proposition 7.

If 𝖧\mathsf{H} satisfies assumptions A.1–A.3, then it is non-negative and uniquely maximized by the uniform distribution 𝐩=𝟏/d{\bm{p}}=\mathbf{1}/d.

That is, assumptions A.1-A.3 ensure that the uniform distribution is the maximum entropy distribution. A particular case of generalized entropies satisfying assumptions A.1–A.3 are uniformly separable functions of the form 𝖧⁡(𝒑)=∑j=1dh⁡(pj)\mathsf{H}({\bm{p}})=\sum_{j=1}^{d}h(p_{j}), where h:[0,1]→ℝ+h:[0,1]\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}_{+} is a non-negative strictly concave function such that h⁡(0)=h⁡(1)=0h(0)=h(1)=0. However, our framework is not restricted to this form.

Induced Fenchel-Young loss.

If the ground truth is 𝒚=𝒆k{\bm{y}}=\bm{e}_{k} and assumption A.1 holds, the Fenchel-Young loss definition (18) becomes

L−𝖧​(𝜽,𝒆k)=(−𝖧)∗​(𝜽)−θk.L_{-\mathsf{H}}(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{k})=(-\mathsf{H})^{*}(\bm{\theta})-\theta_{k}. (45)

This form was also recently proposed by Duchi et al. (2018, Proposition 3). By using the fact that Ω∗​(𝜽+c​𝟏)=Ω∗​(𝜽)+c\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta}+c\bm{1})=\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta})+c for all c∈ℝc\in{\mathbb{R}} if 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)⊆△d\dom(\Omega)\subseteq\triangle^{d}, we can further rewrite it as

L−𝖧​(𝜽,𝒆k)=(−𝖧)∗​(𝜽−θk​𝟏).L_{-\mathsf{H}}(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{k})=(-\mathsf{H})^{*}(\bm{\theta}-\theta_{k}\bm{1}). (46)

This expression shows that Fenchel-Young losses over △d\triangle^{d} can be written solely in terms of the generalized “cumulant function” (−𝖧)∗(-\mathsf{H})^{*}. Indeed, when 𝖧\mathsf{H} is Shannon’s entropy, we recover the cumulant (a.k.a. log-partition) function (−𝖧s)∗(𝜽)=log∑i=1dexp(θi)(-\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{s}})^{*}(\bm{\theta})=\log\sum_{i=1}^{d}\exp(\theta_{i}). When 𝖧\mathsf{H} is strongly concave over △d\triangle^{d}, we can also see (−𝖧)∗(-\mathsf{H})^{*} as a smoothed max operator (Nesterov, 2005; Niculae and Blondel, 2017; Mensch and Blondel, 2018) and hence L−𝖧​(𝜽,𝒆k)L_{-\mathsf{H}}(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{k}) can be seen as a smoothed upper-bound of the perceptron loss (𝜽;𝒆k)↦maxi∈[d]⁡θi−θk(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{k})\mapsto\max_{i\in[d]}\theta_{i}-\theta_{k}.

It is well-known that minimizing the logistic loss (𝜽;𝒆k)↦log∑iexpθi−θk(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{k})\mapsto\log\sum_{i}\exp\theta_{i}-\theta_{k} is equivalent to minimizing the 𝖪𝖫\mathsf{KL} divergence between 𝒆k\bm{e}_{k} and 𝗌𝗈𝖿𝗍𝗆𝖺𝗑(𝜽)\softmax(\bm{\theta}), which in turn is equivalent to maximizing the likelihood of the ground-truth label, 𝗌𝗈𝖿𝗍𝗆𝖺𝗑(𝜽)k\softmax(\bm{\theta})_{k}. Importantly, this equivalence does not carry over for generalized entropies 𝖧\mathsf{H}: minimizing L−𝖧​(𝜽,𝒆k)L_{-\mathsf{H}}(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{k}) is not in general equivalent to minimizing B−𝖧​(𝒆k,𝒚^−𝖧​(𝜽))B_{-\mathsf{H}}(\bm{e}_{k},\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{-\mathsf{H}}(\bm{\theta})) or maximizing 𝒚^−𝖧​(𝜽)k\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{-\mathsf{H}}(\bm{\theta})_{k}. In fact, maximizing the likelihood is generally a non-concave problem. Fenchel-Young losses can be seen as a principled way to construct a convex loss regardless of 𝖧\mathsf{H}.

4.2 Expected loss, Bayes risk and Fisher consistency

Let YY be a random variable taking values in 𝒴={𝒆i}i=1d{\mathcal{Y}}=\{\bm{e}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{d}. If 𝖧\mathsf{H} satisfies assumption A.1, we can use (45) to obtain simpler expressions of the expected loss and pointwise Bayes risk than the ones derived in §3.3.

Expected loss.

Indeed, the expected loss (risk) for all 𝒑∈△d{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d} simplifies to:

𝔼𝒑​[L−𝖧​(𝜽,Y)]=∑i=1dpi​L−𝖧​(𝜽,𝒆i)=∑i=1dpi​((−𝖧)∗​(𝜽)−θj)=(−𝖧)∗​(𝜽)−⟨𝒑,𝜽⟩.{\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[L_{-\mathsf{H}}(\bm{\theta};Y)]=\sum_{i=1}^{d}p_{i}L_{-\mathsf{H}}(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{i})=\sum_{i=1}^{d}p_{i}((-\mathsf{H})^{*}(\bm{\theta})-\theta_{j})=(-\mathsf{H})^{*}(\bm{\theta})-{\langle{\bm{p}},\bm{\theta}\rangle}. (47)

Bayes risk and entropy.

The pointwise (conditional) Bayes risk thus becomes

min𝜽∈ℝd⁡𝔼𝒑​[L−𝖧​(𝜽,Y)]=min𝜽∈ℝd⁡(−𝖧)∗​(𝜽)−⟨𝒑,𝜽⟩=𝖧⁡(𝒑).\min_{\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}{\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[L_{-\mathsf{H}}(\bm{\theta};Y)]=\min_{\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}(-\mathsf{H})^{*}(\bm{\theta})-{\langle{\bm{p}},\bm{\theta}\rangle}=\mathsf{H}({\bm{p}}). (48)

Therefore, the pointwise Bayes risk is equal to the generalized entropy 𝖧\mathsf{H} generating L−𝖧L_{-\mathsf{H}}, evaluated at 𝒑{\bm{p}}. This is consistent with (38), which states that the pointwise Bayes risk is equal to the Bregman information of YY under 𝒑{\bm{p}}, because

𝕀−𝖧​(Y,𝒑)=−𝕀𝖧​(Y,𝒑)=𝖧⁡(𝔼𝒑​[Y])−𝔼𝒑​[𝖧⁡(Y)]=𝖧⁡(𝒑),{\mathbb{I}}_{-\mathsf{H}}(Y;{\bm{p}})=-{\mathbb{I}}_{\mathsf{H}}(Y;{\bm{p}})=\mathsf{H}({\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[Y])-{\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[\mathsf{H}(Y)]=\mathsf{H}({\bm{p}}), (49)

where we used 𝔼𝒑​[Y]=𝒑{\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[Y]={\bm{p}} and assumption A.1.

A similar relation between generalized entropies and pointwise (conditional) Bayes risk is well-known in the proper loss (scoring rule) literature (Grünwald and Dawid, 2004; Gneiting and Raftery, 2007; Reid and Williamson, 2010; Williamson et al., 2016). The main difference is that the minimization above is over ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, while it is over △d\triangle^{d} in that literature (§10.1). As noted by Reid and Williamson (2011, §4.6), Bregman information can also be connected the notion of statistical information developed by DeGroot (1962), the reduction between prior and posterior uncertainty 𝖧\mathsf{H}, of which mutual information is a special case.

Fisher consistency.

From (47), 𝔼𝒑​[L−𝖧​(𝜽,Y)]=L−𝖧​(𝜽,𝒑)+Ω⁡(𝒑){\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[L_{-\mathsf{H}}(\bm{\theta};Y)]=L_{-\mathsf{H}}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{p}})+\Omega({\bm{p}}). Combined with Proposition 4, we have that the pointwise Bayes risk (48) is achieved if and only if 𝒚^−𝖧​(𝜽)=𝒑\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{-\mathsf{H}}(\bm{\theta})={\bm{p}}. Such losses are Fisher consistent estimators of probabilities (Williamson et al., 2016).

4.3 Examples

We now give examples of generalized entropies over the simplex △d\triangle^{d} (we omit the indicator function I△dI_{\triangle^{d}} from the definitions since there is no ambiguity). We illustrate them together with the regularized prediction function and loss they produce in Figure 4. Several of the resulting loss functions are new to our knowledge.

Shannon entropy (Shannon and Weaver, 1949).

This is the foundation of information theory, defined as

𝖧s(𝒑)≔−∑j=1dpjlogpj.\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{s}}({\bm{p}})\coloneqq-\sum_{j=1}^{d}p_{j}\log p_{j}. (50)

As seen in Table 1, the resulting Fenchel-Young loss L−𝖧sL_{-\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{s}}} corresponds to the logistic loss. The associated distribution is the classical softmax, Eq. (10).

Tsallis α\alpha-entropies (Tsallis, 1988).

These entropies are defined as

𝖧αt​(𝒑)≔k​(α−1)−1​(1−∑j=1dpjα),\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{t}}_{\alpha}({\bm{p}})\coloneqq k(\alpha-1)^{-1}\left(1-\sum_{j=1}^{d}p_{j}^{\alpha}\right), (51)

where α≥0\alpha\geq 0 and kk is an arbitrary positive constant. They arise as a generalization of the Shannon-Khinchin axioms to non-extensive systems (Suyari, 2004) and have numerous scientific applications (Gell-Mann and Tsallis, 2004; Martins et al., 2009a). For convenience, we set k=α−1k=\alpha^{-1} for the rest of this paper. Tsallis entropies satisfy assumptions A.1–A.3 and can also be written in separable form:

𝖧αt​(𝒑)≔∑j=1dhα​(pj)withhα​(t)≔t−tαα⁡(α−1).\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{t}}_{\alpha}({\bm{p}})\coloneqq\sum_{j=1}^{d}h_{\alpha}(p_{j})\quad\text{with}\quad h_{\alpha}(t)\coloneqq\frac{t-t^{\alpha}}{\alpha(\alpha-1)}. (52)

The limit case α→1\alpha\rightarrow 1 corresponds to the Shannon entropy. When α=2\alpha=2, we recover the Gini index (Gini, 1912), a popular “impurity measure” for decision trees:

𝖧2t​(𝒑)=12​∑j=1dpj​(1−pj)=12​(1−‖𝒑‖22)∀𝒑∈△d.\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{t}}_{2}({\bm{p}})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{d}p_{j}(1-p_{j})=\frac{1}{2}(1-\|{\bm{p}}\|_{2}^{2})\quad\forall{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d}. (53)

Using the constant invariance property in Proposition 4, it can be checked that L−𝖧2tL_{-\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{t}}_{2}} recovers the sparsemax loss (Martins and Astudillo, 2016) (cf. Table 1).

Another interesting case is α→+∞\alpha\rightarrow+\infty, which gives 𝖧∞t​(𝒑)=0\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{t}}_{\infty}({\bm{p}})=0, hence L−𝖧∞tL_{-\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{t}}_{\infty}} is the perceptron loss in Table 1. The resulting “𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑\argmax” distribution puts all probability mass on the top-scoring classes. In summary, the prediction functions for α=1,2,∞\alpha=1,2,\infty are respectively 𝗌𝗈𝖿𝗍𝗆𝖺𝗑\softmax, 𝗌𝗉𝖺𝗋𝗌𝖾𝗆𝖺𝗑\sparsemax, and 𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑\argmax. Tsallis entropies can therefore be seen as a continuous parametric family subsuming these important cases.

Norm entropies.

An interesting class of non-separable entropies are entropies generated by a qq-norm, defined as

𝖧qn​(𝒑)≔1−‖𝒑‖q.\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{n}}_{q}({\bm{p}})\coloneqq 1-\|{\bm{p}}\|_{q}. (54)

We call them norm entropies. By the Minkowski inequality, qq-norms with q>1q>1 are strictly convex on the simplex, so 𝖧qn\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{n}}_{q} satisfies assumptions A.1–A.3 for q>1q>1. The resulting norm entropies differ from Tsallis entropies in that the norm is not raised to the power of qq: a subtle but important difference. The limit case q→∞q\rightarrow\infty is particularly interesting: in this case, we obtain 𝖧n∞=1−∥⋅∥∞\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{n}}_{\infty}=1-\|\cdot\|_{\infty}, recovering the Berger-Parker dominance index (Berger and Parker, 1970), widely used in ecology to measure species diversity. We surprisingly encounter 𝖧∞n\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{n}}_{\infty} again in Section 5, as a limit case for the existence of separation margins.

Squared norm entropies.

Inspired by Niculae and Blondel (2017), as a simple extension of the Gini index (53), we consider the generalized entropy based on squared qq-norms:

𝖧qsq​(𝒑)≔12​(1−‖𝒑‖q2)=12−12​(∑j=1dpjq)2q.\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{sq}}_{q}({\bm{p}})\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}(1-\|{\bm{p}}\|^{2}_{q})=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{d}p_{j}^{q}\right)^{\frac{2}{q}}. (55)

The constant term 12\frac{1}{2}, omitted by Niculae and Blondel (2017), ensures satisfaction of A.1. For q∈(1,2]q\in(1,2], it is known that the squared qq-norm is strongly convex w.r.t. ∥⋅∥q\|\cdot\|_{q} (Ball et al., 1994), implying that (−𝖧qsq)∗(-\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{sq}}_{q})^{*}, and therefore L−𝖧qsqL_{-\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{sq}}_{q}}, is smooth. Although 𝒚^−𝖧qsq​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{-\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{sq}}_{q}}(\bm{\theta}) cannot to our knowledge be solved in closed form for q∈(1,2)q\in(1,2), efficient iterative algorithms such as projected gradient are available.

Rényi 𝜷\beta-entropies.

Rényi entropies (Rényi, 1961) are defined for any β≥0\beta\geq 0 as:

𝖧βr​(𝒑)≔11−β​log​∑j=1dpjβ.\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{r}}_{\beta}({\bm{p}})\coloneqq\frac{1}{1-\beta}\log\sum_{j=1}^{d}p_{j}^{\beta}. (56)

Unlike Shannon and Tsallis entropies, Rényi entropies are not separable, with the exception of β→1\beta\rightarrow 1, which also recovers Shannon entropy as a limit case. The case β→+∞\beta\rightarrow+\infty gives 𝖧βr​(𝒑)=−log⁡‖𝒑‖∞\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{r}}_{\beta}({\bm{p}})=-\log\|{\bm{p}}\|_{\infty}. For β∈[0,1]\beta\in[0,1], Rényi entropies satisfy assumptions A.1–A.3; for β>1\beta>1, Rényi entropies fail to be concave. They are however pseudo-concave (Mangasarian, 1965), meaning that, for all 𝒑,𝒒∈△d{\bm{p}},\bm{q}\in\triangle^{d}, ⟨∇𝖧βr​(𝒑),𝒒−𝒑⟩≤0{\langle\nabla\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{r}}_{\beta}({\bm{p}}),\bm{q}-{\bm{p}}\rangle}\leq 0 implies 𝖧βr​(𝒒)≤𝖧βr​(𝒑)\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{r}}_{\beta}(\bm{q})\leq\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{r}}_{\beta}({\bm{p}}). This implies, among other things, that points 𝒑∈△d{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d} with zero gradient are maximizers of ⟨𝒑,𝜽⟩+𝖧βr​(𝒑){\langle{\bm{p}},\bm{\theta}\rangle}+\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{r}}_{\beta}({\bm{p}}), which allows us to compute the predictive distribution 𝒚^−𝖧βr\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{-\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{r}}_{\beta}} with gradient-based methods.

4.4 Binary classification case

When d=2d=2, the convex conjugate expression simplifies and reduces to a univariate maximization problem over [0,1][0,1]:

Ω∗​(𝜽)=max𝒑∈△2⁡⟨𝜽,𝒑⟩−Ω⁡(𝒑)=maxp∈[0,1]⁡θ1​p+θ2​(1−p)−Ω⁡([p,1−p])=ϕ∗​(θ1−θ2)+θ2,\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta})=\max_{{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{2}}{\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{p}}\rangle}-\Omega({\bm{p}})=\max_{p\in[0,1]}\theta_{1}p+\theta_{2}(1-p)-\Omega([p,1-p])=\phi^{*}(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2})+\theta_{2}, (57)

where we defined ϕ⁡(p)≔Ω⁡([p,1−p])\phi(p)\coloneqq\Omega([p,1-p]). Likewise, it is easy to verify that we also have Ω∗​(𝜽)=ϕ∗​(θ2−θ1)+θ1\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta})=\phi^{*}(\theta_{2}-\theta_{1})+\theta_{1}. Let us choose 𝜽=[s,−s]∈ℝ2\bm{\theta}=[s,-s]\in{\mathbb{R}}^{2} for some s∈ℝs\in{\mathbb{R}}. Since the ground truth is 𝒚∈{𝒆1,𝒆2}{\bm{y}}\in\{\bm{e}_{1},\bm{e}_{2}\}, where 𝒆1\bm{e}_{1} and 𝒆2\bm{e}_{2} represent positive and negative classes, from (46), we can write

LΩ​(𝜽,𝒆j)=Ω∗​(𝜽−θj​𝟏)={Ω∗​([0,−s])=ϕ∗​(−s) if ​j=1Ω∗​([s,0])=ϕ∗​(s) if ​j=2.L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{j})=\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta}-\theta_{j}\bm{1})=\begin{cases}\Omega^{*}([0,-s])=\phi^{*}(-s)&\mbox{ if }j=1\\ \Omega^{*}([s,0])=\phi^{*}(s)&\mbox{ if }j=2\end{cases}. (58)

This can be written concisely as ϕ∗​(−y​s)\phi^{*}(-ys) where y∈{+1,−1}y\in\{+1,-1\}. Losses that can be written in this form are sometimes called margin losses (Reid and Williamson, 2010). These are losses that treat the positive and negative classes symmetrically. We have thus made a connection between margin losses and the regularization function ϕ⁡(p)≔Ω⁡([p,1−p])\phi(p)\coloneqq\Omega([p,1-p]). Note, however, that this is different from the notion of margin we develop in §5.

Examples.

Choosing ϕ⁡(p)=−𝖧s​([p,1−p])\phi(p)=-\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{s}}([p,1-p]) leads to the binary logistic loss

ϕ∗​(−y​s)=log⁡(1+exp⁡(−y​s)).\phi^{*}(-ys)=\log(1+\exp(-ys)). (59)

Choosing ϕ⁡(p)=−𝖧2t​([p,1−p])=p2−p\phi(p)=-\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{t}}_{2}([p,1-p])=p^{2}-p leads to

ϕ∗​(u)={0 if ​u≤−1u if ​u≥114​(u+1)2 o.w. .\phi^{*}(u)=\begin{cases}0&\mbox{ if }u\leq-1\\ u&\mbox{ if }u\geq 1\\ \frac{1}{4}(u+1)^{2}&\mbox{ o.w. }\end{cases}. (60)

The resulting loss, ϕ⁡(−y​s)\phi(-ys), is known as the modified Huber loss in the literature (Zhang, 2004). Hence, the sparsemax loss is the multiclass extension of the modified Huber loss, as as already noted in (Martins and Astudillo, 2016).

Finally, we note that the modified Huber loss is closely related to the smoothed hinge loss (Shalev-Shwartz and Zhang, 2016). Indeed, choosing ϕ⁡(p)=12​p2−p\phi(p)=\frac{1}{2}p^{2}-p (notice the 12\frac{1}{2} factor), we obtain

ϕ∗​(u)={0 if ​u≤−1u+12 if ​u≥012​(1+u)2 o.w. .\phi^{*}(u)=\begin{cases}0&\mbox{ if }u\leq-1\\ u+\frac{1}{2}&\mbox{ if }u\geq 0\\ \frac{1}{2}(1+u)^{2}&\mbox{ o.w. }\end{cases}. (61)

It can be verified that ϕ∗​(−y​s)\phi^{*}(-ys) is indeed the smoothed hinge loss.

5 Separation margin of Fenchel-Young losses

In this section, we are going to see that the simple assumptions A.1–A.3 about a generalized entropy 𝖧\mathsf{H} are enough to obtain results about the separation margin associated with L−𝖧L_{-\mathsf{H}}. The notion of margin is well-known in machine learning, lying at the heart of support vector machines and leading to generalization error bounds (Vapnik, 1998; Schölkopf and Smola, 2002; Guermeur, 2007). We provide a definition and will see that many other Fenchel-Young losses also have a “margin,” for suitable conditions on 𝖧\mathsf{H}. Then, we take a step further, and connect the existence of a margin with the sparsity of the regularized prediction function, providing necessary and sufficient conditions for Fenchel-Young losses to have a margin. Finally, we show how this margin can be computed analytically.

Definition 8.

Separation margin

Let L⁡(𝛉,𝐞k)L(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{k}) be a loss function over ℝd×{𝐞i}i=1d{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\times\{\bm{e}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{d}. We say that LL has the separation margin property if there exists m>0m>0 such that:

θk≥m+maxj≠k⁡θj⇒L⁡(𝜽,𝒆k)=0.\theta_{k}\geq m+\max_{j\neq k}\theta_{j}\quad\Rightarrow\quad L(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{k})=0. (62)

The smallest possible mm that satisfies (62) is called the margin of LL, denoted margin⁡(L)\mathrm{margin}(L).

Examples.

The most famous example of a loss with a separation margin is the multi-class hinge loss, L⁡(𝜽,𝒆k)=max⁡{0,maxj≠k⁡1+θj−θk}L(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{k})=\max\{0,\max_{j\neq k}1+\theta_{j}-\theta_{k}\}, which we saw in Table 1 to be a Fenchel-Young loss: it is immediate from the definition that its margin is 11. Less trivially, Martins and Astudillo (2016, Prop. 3.5) showed that the sparsemax loss also has the separation margin property. On the negative side, the logistic loss does not have a margin, as it is strictly positive. Characterizing which Fenchel-Young losses have a margin is an important question which we address next.

Conditions for existence of margin.

To accomplish our goal, we need to characterize the gradient mappings ∂(−𝖧)\partial(-\mathsf{H}) and ∇(−𝖧)∗\nabla(-\mathsf{H})^{*} associated with generalized entropies (note that ∂(−𝖧)\partial(-\mathsf{H}) is never single-valued: if 𝜽\bm{\theta} is in ∂(−𝖧)​(𝒑)\partial(-\mathsf{H})(\bm{p}), then so is 𝜽+c​𝟏\bm{\theta}+c\mathbf{1}, for any constant c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}). Of particular importance is the subdifferential set ∂(−𝖧)​(𝒆k)\partial(-\mathsf{H})(\bm{e}_{k}). The next proposition, whose proof we defer to §B.4, uses this set to provide a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of a separation margin, along with a formula for computing it.

Proposition 9.

Let 𝖧\mathsf{H} satisfy A.1–A.3. Then:

  1. 1.

    The loss L−𝖧L_{-\mathsf{H}} has a separation margin iff there is a m>0m>0 such that m​𝒆k∈∂(−𝖧)​(𝒆k)m\bm{e}_{k}\in\partial(-\mathsf{H})(\bm{e}_{k}).

  2. 2.

    If the above holds, then the margin of L−𝖧L_{-\mathsf{H}} is given by the smallest such mm or, equivalently,

    margin⁡(L−𝖧)=sup𝒑∈△d𝖧⁡(𝒑)1−‖𝒑‖∞.\mathrm{margin}(L_{-\mathsf{H}})=\sup_{{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d}}\frac{\mathsf{H}({\bm{p}})}{1-\|{\bm{p}}\|_{\infty}}. (63)

Reassuringly, the first part confirms that the logistic loss does not have a margin, since ∂(−𝖧s)​(𝒆k)=∅\partial(-\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{s}})(\bm{e}_{k})=\varnothing. A second interesting fact is that the denominator of (63) is the generalized entropy 𝖧∞n​(𝒑)\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{n}}_{\infty}({\bm{p}}) introduced in §4: the ∞\infty-norm entropy. As Figure 4 suggests, this entropy provides an upper bound for convex losses with unit margin. This provides some intuition to the formula (63), which seeks a distribution 𝒑{\bm{p}} maximizing the entropy ratio between 𝖧⁡(𝒑)\mathsf{H}({\bm{p}}) and 𝖧∞n​(𝒑)\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{n}}_{\infty}({\bm{p}}).

Relationship between sparsity and margins.

The next result, proved in §B.5, characterizes more precisely the image of ∇(−𝖧)∗\nabla(-\mathsf{H})^{*}. In doing so, it establishes a key result in this paper: a sufficient condition for the existence of a separation margin in L−𝖧L_{-\mathsf{H}} is the sparsity of the regularized prediction function y^−𝖧≡∇(−𝖧)∗\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{-\mathsf{H}}\equiv\nabla(-\mathsf{H})^{*}, i.e., its ability to reach the entire simplex, including the boundary points. If 𝖧\mathsf{H} is uniformly separable, this is also a necessary condition.

Proposition 10.

Relationship between margin losses and sparse predictive probabilities

Let 𝖧\mathsf{H} satisfy A.1–A.3 and be uniformly separable, i.e., 𝖧⁡(𝐩)=∑i=1dh⁡(pi)\mathsf{H}({\bm{p}})=\sum_{i=1}^{d}h(p_{i}). Then the following statements are all equivalent:

  1. 1.

    ∂(−𝖧)​(𝒑)≠∅\partial(-\mathsf{H})({\bm{p}})\neq\varnothing for any 𝒑∈△d{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d};

  2. 2.

    The mapping ∇(−𝖧)∗\nabla(-\mathsf{H})^{*} covers the full simplex, i.e., ∇(−𝖧)∗​(ℝd)=△d\nabla(-\mathsf{H})^{*}({\mathbb{R}}^{d})=\triangle^{d};

  3. 3.

    L−𝖧L_{-\mathsf{H}} has the separation margin property.

For a general 𝖧\mathsf{H} (not necessarily separable) satisfying A.1–A.3, we have (1) ⇔\Leftrightarrow (2) ⇒\Rightarrow (3).

Let us reflect for a moment on the three conditions stated in Proposition 10. The first two conditions involve the subdifferential and gradient of −𝖧-\mathsf{H} and its conjugate; the third condition is the margin property of L−𝖧L_{-\mathsf{H}}. To provide some intuition, consider the case where 𝖧\mathsf{H} is separable with 𝖧⁡(𝒑)=∑ih⁡(pi)\mathsf{H}({\bm{p}})=\sum_{i}h(p_{i}) and hh is differentiable in (0,1)(0,1). Then, from the concavity of hh, its derivative h′h^{\prime} is decreasing, hence the first condition is met if limt=0+h′​(t)<∞\lim_{t=0^{+}}h^{\prime}(t)<\infty and limt=1−h′​(t)>−∞\lim_{t=1^{-}}h^{\prime}(t)>-\infty. This is the case with Tsallis entropies for α>1\alpha>1, but not Shannon entropy, since h′​(t)=−1−log⁡th^{\prime}(t)=-1-\log t explodes at 00. As stated in Definition 5, functions whose gradient “explodes” in the boundary of their domain (hence failing to meet the first condition in Proposition 10) are called “essentially smooth” (Rockafellar, 1970). For those functions, ∇(−𝖧)∗\nabla(-\mathsf{H})^{*} maps only to the relative interior of △d\triangle^{d}, never attaining boundary points (Wainwright and Jordan, 2008); this is expressed in the second condition. This prevents essentially smooth functions from generating a sparse 𝒚−𝖧≡∇(−𝖧)∗{\bm{y}}_{-\mathsf{H}}\equiv\nabla(-\mathsf{H})^{*} or (if they are separable) a loss L−𝖧L_{-\mathsf{H}} with a margin, as asserted by the third condition. Since Legendre-type functions (Definition 5) are strictly convex and essentially smooth, by Proposition 6, loss functions for which the composite form L−𝖧(𝜽;𝒚)=B−𝖧(𝒚∥𝒚^−𝖧(𝜽))L_{-\mathsf{H}}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=B_{-\mathsf{H}}({\bm{y}}\|\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{-\mathsf{H}}(\bm{\theta})) holds, which is the case of the logistic loss but not of the sparsemax loss, do not enjoy a margin and cannot induce a sparse probability distribution. This is geometrically visible in Figure 4.

Margin computation.

For Fenchel-Young losses that have the separation margin property, Proposition 9 provided a formula for determining the margin. While informative, formula (63) is not very practical, as it involves a generally non-convex optimization problem. The next proposition, proved in §B.6, takes a step further and provides a remarkably simple closed-form expression for generalized entropies that are twice-differentiable. To simplify notation, we denote by ∇j𝖧​(𝒑)≡(∇𝖧​(𝒑))j\nabla_{j}\mathsf{H}({\bm{p}})\equiv(\nabla\mathsf{H}({\bm{p}}))_{j} the jthj^{\text{th}} component of ∇𝖧​(𝒑)\nabla\mathsf{H}({\bm{p}}).

Proposition 11.

Assume 𝖧\mathsf{H} satisfies the conditions in Proposition 10 and is twice-differentiable on the simplex. Then, for arbitrary j≠kj\neq k:

margin⁡(L−𝖧)=∇j𝖧​(𝒆k)−∇k𝖧​(𝒆k).\mathrm{margin}(L_{-\mathsf{H}})={\nabla_{j}{\mathsf{H}}(\bm{e}_{k})}-{\nabla_{k}{\mathsf{H}}(\bm{e}_{k})}. (64)

In particular, if 𝖧\mathsf{H} is separable, i.e., 𝖧⁡(𝐩)=∑i=1|𝒴|h⁡(pi)\mathsf{H}({\bm{p}})=\sum_{i=1}^{|{\mathcal{Y}}|}h(p_{i}), where h:[0,1]→ℝ+h:[0,1]\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}_{+} is concave, twice differentiable, with h⁡(0)=h⁡(1)=0h(0)=h(1)=0, then

margin(L−𝖧)=h′(0)−h′(1)=−∫01h′′(t)dt.\mathrm{margin}(L_{-\mathsf{H}})=h^{\prime}(0)-h^{\prime}(1)=-\hskip-0.86108pt\int_{0}^{1}\hskip-1.72218pth^{\prime\prime}(t)dt. (65)

The compact formula (64) provides a geometric characterization of separable entropies and their margins: (65) tells us that only the slopes of hh at the two extremities of [0,1][0,1] are relevant in determining the margin.

Example: case of Tsallis and norm entropies.

As seen in §4, Tsallis entropies are separable with h⁡(t)=(t−tα)/(α⁡(α−1))h(t)=(t-t^{\alpha})/(\alpha(\alpha-1)). For α>1\alpha>1, h′​(t)=(1−α​tα−1)/(α⁡(α−1))h^{\prime}(t)=(1-\alpha t^{\alpha-1})/(\alpha(\alpha-1)), hence h′​(0)=1/(α⁡(α−1))h^{\prime}(0)=1/(\alpha(\alpha-1)) and h′(1)=−1/αh^{\prime}(1)=-1/\alpha. Proposition 11 then yields

margin⁡(L−𝖧αt)=h′​(0)−h′​(1)=(α−1)−1.\mathrm{margin}(L_{-\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{t}}_{\alpha}})=h^{\prime}(0)-h^{\prime}(1)=(\alpha-1)^{-1}. (66)

Norm entropies, while not separable, have gradient ∇𝖧qn​(𝒑)=−(𝒑/‖𝒑‖q)q−1\nabla\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{n}}_{q}({\bm{p}})=-(\nicefrac{{{\bm{p}}}}{{\|{\bm{p}}\|_{q}}})^{q-1}, giving ∇𝖧qn​(𝒆k)=−𝒆k\nabla\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{n}}_{q}(\bm{e}_{k})=-\bm{e}_{k}, so

margin⁡(𝖧qn)=∇j𝖧qn​(𝒆k)−∇k𝖧qn​(𝒆k)=1,\mathrm{margin}(\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{n}}_{q})=\nabla_{j}\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{n}}_{q}(\bm{e}_{k})-\nabla_{k}\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{n}}_{q}(\bm{e}_{k})=1, (67)

as confirmed visually in Figure 4, in the binary case.

6 Positive measure prediction with Fenchel-Young losses

In this section, we again restrict to classification and 𝒴={𝒆i}i=1d{\mathcal{Y}}=\{\bm{e}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{d} but now assume that 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)⊆𝖼𝗈𝗇𝖾(𝒴)=ℝ+d\dom(\Omega)\subseteq\cone({\mathcal{Y}})={\mathbb{R}}^{d}_{+}, where 𝖼𝗈𝗇𝖾(𝒴)\cone({\mathcal{Y}}) is the conic hull of 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}}. In this case, the regularized prediction function (8) becomes

𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)∈𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑𝐦∈ℝ+d⟨𝜽,𝐦⟩−Ω⁡(𝐦),\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})\in\argmax_{{\bm{m}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}_{+}}{{\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{m}}\rangle}}-\Omega({\bm{m}}), (68)

where 𝜽∈ℝd\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} is again a vector of prediction scores and 𝒎∈ℝ+d{\bm{m}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}_{+} can be interpreted as a discrete positive measure (unnormalized probability distribution).

We first demonstrate how Fenchel-Young losses over positive measures allow to recover one-vs-all reductions (§6.1), theoretically justifying this popular scheme. We then give examples of loss instantiations (§6.2).

6.1 Uniformly separable regularizers and one-vs-all loss functions

A particularly simple case is that of uniformly separable Ω\Omega, i.e., Ω⁡(𝒎)=∑j=1dϕ⁡(mj)+Iℝ+d​(𝒎)\Omega({\bm{m}})=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\phi(m_{j})+I_{{\mathbb{R}}_{+}^{d}}({\bm{m}}), for some ϕ:ℝ+→ℝ\phi\colon{\mathbb{R}}_{+}\to{\mathbb{R}}. In that case the regularized prediction function can be computed in a coordinate-wise fashion:

(𝒚^Ω​(𝜽))j=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑m∈ℝ+m​θj−ϕ⁡(m).(\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}))_{j}=\argmax_{m\in{\mathbb{R}}_{+}}~m\theta_{j}-\phi(m). (69)

As we shall later see, this simplified optimization problem often enjoys a closed-form solution. Intuitively, (𝒚^Ω​(𝜽))j(\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}))_{j} can be interpreted as the “unnormalized probability” of class jj. Likewise, the corresponding Fenchel-Young loss is separable over classes:

LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)=Ω∗​(𝜽)+Ω⁡(𝒚)−⟨𝜽,𝒚⟩=∑j=1dϕ∗​(θj)+ϕ⁡(yj)−θj​yj=∑j=1dLϕ​(θj,yj),L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta})+\Omega({\bm{y}})-{\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{y}}\rangle}=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\phi^{*}(\theta_{j})+\phi(y_{j})-\theta_{j}y_{j}=\sum_{j=1}^{d}L_{\phi}(\theta_{j};y_{j}), (70)

where yj∈{1,0}y_{j}\in\{1,0\} indicates membership to class jj. The separability allows to train the model producing each θj\theta_{j} in an embarrassingly parallel fashion.

Let us now consider the case ϕ⁡(p)=−𝖧⁡([p,1−p])\phi(p)=-\mathsf{H}([p,1-p]), where 𝖧\mathsf{H} is a generalized entropy and ϕ\phi is restricted to [0,1][0,1]. From §4.4, we know that ϕ∗​(s)=ϕ∗​(−s)+s\phi^{*}(s)=\phi^{*}(-s)+s for all s∈ℝs\in{\mathbb{R}}. If 𝖧\mathsf{H} further satisfies assumption A.1, meaning that ϕ⁡(1)=ϕ⁡(0)=0\phi(1)=\phi(0)=0, then we obtain

Lϕ​(s,1)=ϕ∗​(s)+ϕ⁡(1)−s=ϕ∗​(−s)andLϕ​(s,0)=ϕ∗​(s)+ϕ⁡(0)=ϕ∗​(s).L_{\phi}(s;1)=\phi^{*}(s)+\phi(1)-s=\phi^{*}(-s)\quad\text{and}\quad L_{\phi}(s;0)=\phi^{*}(s)+\phi(0)=\phi^{*}(s). (71)

Combining the two, we obtain

LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)=∑j=1dϕ∗​(−(2​yi−1)​θi),L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\phi^{*}(-(2y_{i}-1)\theta_{i}), (72)

where we used that (2​yi−1)∈{+1,−1}(2y_{i}-1)\in\{+1,-1\}. Fenchel-Young losses thus recover classical one-vs-all loss functions. Since Fenchel-Young losses satisfy LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)=0⇔𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)=𝒚L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=0\Leftrightarrow\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})={\bm{y}}, our framework provides a theoretical justification for one-vs-all, a scheme that works well in practice (Rifkin and Klautau, 2004). Further, our framework justifies using 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) as a measure of class membership, as commonly implemented (with post-normalization) in software packages (Pedregosa et al., 2011; Buitinck et al., 2013).

Finally, we point out that in the binary case, choosing 𝜽=[s,−s]\bm{\theta}=[s,-s], we have the relationship

LΩ​(𝜽,𝒆1)=2​ϕ∗​(−s)andLΩ​(𝜽,𝒆2)=2​ϕ∗​(s).L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{1})=2\phi^{*}(-s)\quad\text{and}\quad L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{2})=2\phi^{*}(s). (73)

Thus, we recover the same loss as in §4.4, up to a constant 2 factor (i.e., learning over the simplex △d\triangle^{d} or over the unit cube [0,1]d[0,1]^{d} is equivalent for binary classification).

6.2 Examples

Recall that Ω⁡(𝒎)=∑j=1dϕ⁡(mj)+Iℝ+d​(𝒎)\Omega({\bm{m}})=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\phi(m_{j})+I_{{\mathbb{R}}_{+}^{d}}({\bm{m}}). Choosing ϕ⁡(p)=12​p2\phi(p)=\frac{1}{2}p^{2} gives

𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)=[𝜽]+andLΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)=∑i=1d12​[θi]+2+12​yi2−θi​yi.\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})=[\bm{\theta}]_{+}\quad\text{and}\quad L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\frac{1}{2}[\theta_{i}]_{+}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}y_{i}^{2}-\theta_{i}y_{i}. (74)

Choosing ϕ⁡(p)=−𝖧s​([p,1−p])+I[0,1]​(p)\phi(p)=-\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{s}}([p,1-p])+I_{[0,1]}(p) leads to

𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)=𝗌𝗂𝗀𝗆𝗈𝗂𝖽(𝜽)≔𝟏𝟏+exp⁡(−𝜽),andLΩ​(𝜽,𝐲)=∑i=1dlog⁡(1+exp⁡(−(2​yi−1)​θi))\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})=\sigmoid(\bm{\theta})\coloneqq\frac{\bm{1}}{\bm{1}+\exp(-\bm{\theta})},\quad\text{and}\quad L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\log(1+\exp(-(2y_{i}-1)\theta_{i})) (75)

the classical sigmoid function and the one-vs-all logistic function. Note that −Ω(𝒑)=∑j𝖧s([pj,1−pj])=−∑jpjlogpj+(1−pj)log(1−pj)-\Omega({\bm{p}})=\sum_{j}\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{s}}([p_{j},1-p_{j}])=-\sum_{j}p_{j}\log p_{j}+(1-p_{j})\log(1-p_{j}) is sometimes known as the Fermi-Dirac entropy (Borwein and Lewis, 2010, Commentary of Section 3.3).

Choosing ϕ⁡(p)=−𝖧2t​([p,1−p])+I[0,1]​(p)=p2−p+I[0,1]​(p)\phi(p)=-\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{t}}_{2}([p,1-p])+I_{[0,1]}(p)=p^{2}-p+I_{[0,1]}(p) leads to

(𝒚^Ω​(𝜽))j=(ϕ∗)′​(sj)={0 if ​u≤−11 if ​u≥112​(u+1) o.w. ∀j∈[d].(\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}))_{j}=(\phi^{*})^{\prime}(s_{j})=\begin{cases}0&\mbox{ if }u\leq-1\\ 1&\mbox{ if }u\geq 1\\ \frac{1}{2}(u+1)&\mbox{ o.w. }\end{cases}\quad\forall j\in[d]. (76)

We can think of this function as a “sparse sigmoid”.

7 Structured prediction with Fenchel-Young losses

In this section, we now turn to prediction over the convex hull of a set 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}} of structured objects (sequences, trees, assignments, etc.), represented as dd-dimensional vectors, i.e. 𝒴⊆ℝd{\mathcal{Y}}\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}^{d}. In this case, the regularized prediction function (8) becomes

𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑𝝁∈𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)⟨𝝁,𝜽⟩−Ω⁡(𝝁).\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})=\argmax_{\bm{\mu}\in\conv({\mathcal{Y}})}{\langle\bm{\mu},\bm{\theta}\rangle}-\Omega(\bm{\mu}). (77)

Typically, |𝒴|{|{\mathcal{Y}}|} will be exponential in dd, i.e., d≪|𝒴|d\ll{|{\mathcal{Y}}|}. Because 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)=∑𝒚∈𝒴p⁡(𝒚)​𝒚=𝔼𝒑​[Y]\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})=\sum_{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}p({\bm{y}}){\bm{y}}={\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[Y] for some 𝒑∈△|𝒴|{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{|{\mathcal{Y}}|}, 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) can be interpreted as the expectation under some (not necessarily unique) underlying distribution.

We first discuss the concepts of probability distribution regularization (§7.1) and mean regularization (§7.2), and the implications in terms of computational tractability and identifiability (note that in the unstructured setting, probability distribution and mean regularizations coincide). We then give several examples of polytopes and show how a Fenchel-Young loss can seamlessly be constructed over them given access to regularized prediction functions (§7.3). Finally, we extend the notion of separation margin to the structured setting (§7.4).

7.1 Distribution regularization, marginal inference and structured sparsemax

In this section, we discuss the concept of probability distribution regularization. Our treatment follows closely the variational formulations of exponential families (Barndorff-Nielsen, 1978; Wainwright and Jordan, 2008) and generalized exponential families (Grünwald and Dawid, 2004; Frongillo and Reid, 2014) but adopts the novel viewpoint of regularized prediction functions. We discuss two instances of that framework: the structured counterpart of the softmax, marginal inference, and a new structured counterpart of the sparsemax, structured sparsemax.

Let us start with a probability-space regularized prediction function

𝒚^−𝖧​(𝒔𝜽)=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑𝐩∈△|𝒴|⟨𝐩,𝐬𝜽⟩+𝖧⁡(𝐩),\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{-\mathsf{H}}(\bm{s}_{\bm{\theta}})=\argmax_{{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{|{\mathcal{Y}}|}}{\langle{\bm{p}},\bm{s}_{\bm{\theta}}\rangle}+\mathsf{H}({\bm{p}}), (78)
