where 𝖧\mathsf{H} is a generalized entropy and 𝒔𝜽≔(⟨𝜽,𝒚⟩)𝒚∈𝒴∈ℝ|𝒴|\bm{s}_{\bm{\theta}}\coloneqq({\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{y}}\rangle})_{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{|{\mathcal{Y}}|} is a vector that contains the scores of all possible structures. Note that in the unstructured setting, where 𝒴={𝒆1,…,𝒆d}{\mathcal{Y}}=\{\bm{e}_{1},\dots,\bm{e}_{d}\}, we have 𝒔𝜽=𝜽\bm{s}_{\bm{\theta}}=\bm{\theta} and hence the distinction between 𝜽\bm{\theta} and 𝒔𝜽\bm{s}_{\bm{\theta}} is not necessary. In the structured prediction setting, however, the above optimization problem is defined over a space of size |𝒴|≫d{|{\mathcal{Y}}|}\gg d. The regularized prediction function outputs a probability distribution over structures and from Danskin’s theorem, we have

𝒚^−𝖧​(𝒔𝜽)=∇𝒔𝜽(−𝖧)∗​(𝒔𝜽)=𝒑⋆∈△|𝒴|.\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{-\mathsf{H}}(\bm{s}_{\bm{\theta}})=\nabla_{\bm{s}_{\bm{\theta}}}(-\mathsf{H})^{*}(\bm{s}_{\bm{\theta}})={\bm{p}}^{\star}\in\triangle^{|{\mathcal{Y}}|}. (79)

Using the chain rule, differentiating w.r.t. 𝜽\bm{\theta} instead of 𝒔𝜽\bm{s}_{\bm{\theta}} gives

∇𝜽(−𝖧)∗​(𝒔𝜽)=𝔼𝒑⋆​[Y]∈𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴).\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}(-\mathsf{H})^{*}(\bm{s}_{\bm{\theta}})={\mathbb{E}}_{{\bm{p}}^{\star}}[Y]\in\conv({\mathcal{Y}}). (80)

Therefore, the gradient w.r.t. 𝜽\bm{\theta} corresponds to the mean under 𝒑⋆{\bm{p}}^{\star}. This can be equivalently expressed under our framework by defining a regularization function directly in mean space. Let us define the regularization function Ω\Omega over 𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)\conv({\mathcal{Y}}) as

−Ω⁡(𝝁)≔max𝒑∈△|𝒴|⁡𝖧⁡(𝒑)s.t.𝔼𝒑​[Y]=𝝁.-\Omega(\bm{\mu})\coloneqq\max_{{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{|{\mathcal{Y}}|}}\mathsf{H}({\bm{p}})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[Y]=\bm{\mu}. (81)

That is, among all distributions satisfying the first-moment matching condition 𝔼𝒑​[Y]=𝝁{\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[Y]=\bm{\mu}, we seek the distribution 𝒑⋆{\bm{p}}^{\star} with maximum (generalized) entropy. This allows to make the underlying distribution unique and identifiable. With this choice of Ω\Omega, simple calculations show that the corresponding regularized prediction function is precisely the mean under that distribution:

𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)=∇Ω∗​(𝜽)=𝔼𝒑⋆​[Y]∈𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴).\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})=\nabla\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta})={\mathbb{E}}_{{\bm{p}}^{\star}}[Y]\in\conv({\mathcal{Y}}). (82)

Similar results hold for higher order moments: If Ω∗\Omega^{*} is twice-differentiable, the Hessian corresponds to the second moment under 𝒑⋆{\bm{p}}^{\star}:

cov𝒑⋆​[Y]=∇2Ω∗​(𝜽).\textnormal{cov}_{{\bm{p}}^{\star}}[Y]=\nabla^{2}\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta}). (83)

The relation between these various maps is summarized in Figure 5.

Marginal inference.

A particular case of (81) is

−Ω⁡(𝝁)=max𝒑∈△|𝒴|⁡𝖧s​(𝒑)s.t.𝔼𝒑​[Y]=𝝁,-\Omega(\bm{\mu})=\max_{{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{|{\mathcal{Y}}|}}\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{s}}({\bm{p}})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[Y]=\bm{\mu}, (84)

where 𝖧s\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{s}} is the Shannon entropy. The distribution achieving maximum Shannon entropy, which is unique, is the Gibbs distribution p⁡(𝒚,𝜽)∝exp⁡(⟨𝜽,𝒚⟩)p({\bm{y}};\bm{\theta})\propto\exp({\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{y}}\rangle}).

As shown in Table 1, the resulting loss LΩL_{\Omega} is the CRF loss (Lafferty et al., 2001) and the resulting regularized prediction function 𝒚^Ω\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega} is known as marginal inference in the literature (Wainwright and Jordan, 2008):

𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)=𝗆𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗂𝗇𝖺𝗅𝗌(𝜽)≔∑𝐲∈𝒴exp⁡(⟨𝜽,𝐲⟩)​𝐲/Z⁡(𝜽),\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})=\marginals(\bm{\theta})\coloneqq\sum_{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}\exp({\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{y}}\rangle}){\bm{y}}\big/Z(\bm{\theta}), (85)

where Z⁡(𝜽)≔∑𝒚∈𝒴exp⁡(⟨𝜽,𝒚⟩)Z(\bm{\theta})\coloneqq\sum_{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}\exp({\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{y}}\rangle}) is the partition function (normalization constant) of the Gibbs distribution. Although marginal inference is intractable in general, we will see in §7.3 that it can be computed exactly and efficiently for specific polytopes. The conjugate of Ω⁡(𝝁)\Omega(\bm{\mu}), Ω∗​(𝜽)\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta}), corresponds to the log partition function: Ω∗​(𝜽)=log⁡Z⁡(𝜽)\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta})=\log Z(\bm{\theta}).

Structured sparsemax.

From the above perspective, it is tempting to define a sparsemax counterpart of the CRF loss and of marginal inference by replacing Shannon’s entropy 𝖧s\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{s}} with the Gini index 𝖧2t\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{t}}_{2} (see (53) for a definition) in (84):

−Ω⁡(𝝁)=max𝒑∈△|𝒴|⁡𝖧2t​(𝒑)s.t.𝔼𝒑​[Y]=𝝁.-\Omega(\bm{\mu})=\max_{{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{|{\mathcal{Y}}|}}\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{t}}_{2}({\bm{p}})\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[Y]=\bm{\mu}. (86)

This is equivalent to seeking a distribution 𝒑⋆{\bm{p}}^{\star} with minimum squared norm

Ω⁡(𝝁)+12=min𝒑∈△|𝒴|⁡12​‖𝒑‖2s.t.𝔼𝒑​[Y]=𝝁.\Omega(\bm{\mu})+\frac{1}{2}=\min_{{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{|{\mathcal{Y}}|}}\frac{1}{2}\|{\bm{p}}\|^{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad{\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[Y]=\bm{\mu}. (87)

The corresponding 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) is then 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)=𝔼𝒑⋆​[Y]\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})={\mathbb{E}}_{{\bm{p}}^{\star}}[Y]. Recalling that 𝒑⋆=𝒚^−𝖧2t​(𝒔𝜽){\bm{p}}^{\star}=\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{-\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{t}}_{2}}(\bm{s}_{\bm{\theta}}), a naive approach would be to first compute the score vector 𝒔𝜽=(⟨𝜽,𝒚⟩)𝒚∈𝒴∈ℝ|𝒴|\bm{s}_{\bm{\theta}}=({\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{y}}\rangle})_{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{|{\mathcal{Y}}|} and then to project that vector on the simplex to obtain 𝒑⋆{\bm{p}}^{\star}. Unfortunately, 𝒔𝜽\bm{s}_{\bm{\theta}} could be exponentially large and 𝒑⋆{\bm{p}}^{\star} could be arbitrarily dense in the worst case, making that approach intractable in general. As also noted by Pillutla et al. (2018), we can approximate the problem by further imposing an upper-bound on the sparsity of the distribution, ‖𝒑‖0≤k\|{\bm{p}}\|_{0}\leq k. Since the optimal kk-sparse distribution solely depends on the top-kk elements of 𝒔𝜽\bm{s}_{\bm{\theta}} (Kyrillidis et al., 2013), we can first use a kk-best oracle to retrieve the top-kk elements of 𝒔𝜽\bm{s}_{\bm{\theta}} and project them onto the simplex. A disadvantage of that approach is that kk-best oracles are usually more complex than MAP oracles and kk could be arbitrarily large in order to guarantee an exact solution to the original problem. For shortest path problems over a directed acyclic graph, an alternative approximation is to smooth the maximum operator directly in the dynamic programming recursion (Mensch and Blondel, 2018).

7.2 Mean regularization and SparseMAP

Marginal inference is computationally tractable only for certain polytopes and structured sparsemax requires approximations, even for polytopes for which exact marginal inference is available. In this section, we discuss an alternative approach which only requires access to a MAP oracle, broadening the set of applicable polytopes. The key idea is mean regularization: We directly regularize the mean 𝝁\bm{\mu} rather than the distribution 𝒑{\bm{p}}.

The mean regularization counterpart of marginal inference is

𝒚^−𝖧s(𝜽)=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑𝝁∈𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)⟨𝜽,𝝁⟩+𝖧s(𝝁)=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝗂𝗇𝝁∈𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)𝖪𝖫(𝝁∥e𝜽−𝟏).\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{-\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{s}}}(\bm{\theta})=\argmax_{\bm{\mu}\in\conv({\mathcal{Y}})}{\langle\bm{\theta},\bm{\mu}\rangle}+\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{s}}(\bm{\mu})=\argmin_{\bm{\mu}\in\conv({\mathcal{Y}})}\mathsf{KL}(\bm{\mu}\|e^{\bm{\theta}-\bm{1}}). (88)

It has been used for specific convex polytopes, most importantly in the optimal transport literature (Cuturi, 2013; Peyré and Cuturi, 2017) but also for learning to predict permutation matrices (Helmbold and Warmuth, 2009) or permutations (Yasutake et al., 2011; Ailon et al., 2016). The mean regularization counterpart of sparsemax is known as SparseMAP (Niculae et al., 2018):

𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)=𝖲𝗉𝖺𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖬𝖠𝖯(𝜽)≔𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑𝝁∈𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)⟨𝜽,𝝁⟩−12​‖𝝁‖2=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝗂𝗇𝝁∈𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)‖𝝁−𝜽‖2.\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})=\sparsemap(\bm{\theta})\coloneqq\argmax_{\bm{\mu}\in\conv({\mathcal{Y}})}{\langle\bm{\theta},\bm{\mu}\rangle}-\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{\mu}\|^{2}=\argmin_{\bm{\mu}\in\conv({\mathcal{Y}})}\|\bm{\mu}-\bm{\theta}\|^{2}. (89)

The main advantage of mean regularization is computational. Indeed, computing 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) now simply involves a dd-dimensional optimization problem instead of a |𝒴||{\mathcal{Y}}|-dimensional one and can be cast as a Bregman projection onto 𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)\conv({\mathcal{Y}})(§3.2). For specific polytopes, that projection can often be computed directly (§7.3). More generally, it can always be computed to arbitrary precision given access to a MAP oracle

𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑𝐲∈𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)⟨𝜽,𝐲⟩=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑𝐲∈𝒴⟨𝜽,𝐲⟩≕𝖬𝖠𝖯(𝜽),\argmax_{{\bm{y}}\in\conv({\mathcal{Y}})}{\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{y}}\rangle}=\argmax_{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}{\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{y}}\rangle}\eqqcolon\map(\bm{\theta}), (90)

thanks to conditional gradient algorithms (§8.3). Since MAP inference is a cornerstone of structured prediction, efficient algorithms have been developed for many kinds of structures (§7.3). In addition, as conditional gradient algorithms maintain a convex combination of vertices, they can also return a (not necessarily unique) distribution 𝒑∈△|𝒴|{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{|{\mathcal{Y}}|} such that 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)=𝔼𝒑​[Y]\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})={\mathbb{E}}_{\bm{p}}[Y]. From Carathéodory’s theorem, the support of 𝒑{\bm{p}} contains at most d≪|𝒴|d\ll|{\mathcal{Y}}| elements. This ensures that 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) can be written as a “small” number of elementary structures. The price to pay for this computational tractability is that the underlying distribution 𝒑{\bm{p}} is not necessarily unique.

7.3 Examples

Deriving loss functions for structured outputs can be challenging. In this section, we give several examples of polytopes 𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)\conv({\mathcal{Y}}) for which efficient computational oracles (MAP, marginal inference, projection) are available, thus allowing to obtain a Fenchel-Young loss for learning over these polytopes. A summary is given in Table 2.

Sequences.

We wish to tag a sequence (𝒙1,…,𝒙n)({\bm{x}}_{1},\dots,{\bm{x}}_{n}) of vectors in ℝp{\mathbb{R}}^{p} (e.g., word representations) with the most likely output sequence (e.g., entity tags) 𝒔=(s1,…,sn)∈[m]n\bm{s}=(s_{1},\dots,s_{n})\in[m]^{n}. It is convenient to represent each sequence 𝒔\bm{s} as a n×m×mn\times m\times m binary tensor 𝒚∈𝒴\bm{y}\in{\mathcal{Y}}, such that yt,i,j=1y_{t,i,j}=1 if 𝒚{\bm{y}} transitions from node jj to node ii on time tt, and 00 otherwise. The potentials 𝜽\bm{\theta} can similarly be organized as a n×m×mn\times m\times m real tensor, such that θt,i,j=ϕt​(𝒙t,i,j)\theta_{t,i,j}=\phi_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t},i,j), where ϕt\phi_{t} is a potential function. Using the above binary tensor representation, the Frobenius inner product ⟨𝜽,𝒚⟩\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{y}}\rangle is equal to ∑t=1nϕt​(𝒙t,st,st−1)\sum_{t=1}^{n}\phi_{t}({\bm{x}}_{t},s_{t},s_{t-1}), the cumulated score of 𝒔\bm{s}.

MAP inference, 𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑𝐲∈𝒴⟨𝐲,𝜽⟩\argmax_{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}{\langle{\bm{y}},\bm{\theta}\rangle}, seeks the highest-scoring sequence and can be computed using Viterbi’s algorithm (Viterbi, 1967) in O⁡(n​m2)O(nm^{2}) time. Marginal inference can be computed in the same cost using the forward-backward algorithm (Baum and Petrie, 1966) or equivalently using backpropagation (Eisner, 2016; Mensch and Blondel, 2018).

When Ω\Omega is defined over 𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)\conv({\mathcal{Y}}) as in (84), the Fenchel-Young loss corresponds to a linear-chain conditional random field loss (Lafferty et al., 2001). In recent years, this loss has been used to train various end-to-end natural language pipelines based on neural networks (Collobert et al., 2011; Lample et al., 2016).

Alignments.

Let 𝑨∈ℝm×p\bm{A}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{m\times p} and 𝑩∈ℝn×p\bm{B}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n\times p} be two time-series of lengths mm and nn, respectively. We denote by 𝒂i∈ℝp\bm{a}_{i}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{p} and 𝒃j∈ℝp\bm{b}_{j}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{p} their ithi^{\text{th}} and jthj^{\text{th}} observations. Our goal is to find an alignment between 𝑨\bm{A} and 𝑩\bm{B}, matching their observations. We define 𝜽\bm{\theta} as a m×nm\times n matrix, such that θi,j\theta_{i,j} is the similarity between observations 𝒂i\bm{a}_{i} and 𝒃j\bm{b}_{j}. Likewise, we represent an alignment 𝒚{\bm{y}} as a m×nm\times n binary matrix, such that yi,j=1y_{i,j}=1 if 𝒂i\bm{a}_{i} is aligned with 𝒃j\bm{b}_{j}, and 00 otherwise. We write 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}} the set of all monotonic alignment matrices, such that the path that connects the upper-left (1,1)(1,1) matrix entry to the lower-right (m,n)(m,n) one uses only ↓,→,↘\downarrow,\rightarrow,\searrow moves.

In this setting, MAP inference, 𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑𝐲∈𝒴⟨𝐲,𝜽⟩\argmax_{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}{\langle{\bm{y}},\bm{\theta}\rangle}, corresponds to seeking the maximal similarity (or equivalently, minimal cost) alignment between the two time-series. It can be computed in O⁡(m​n)O(mn) time using dynamic time warping, DTW (Sakoe and Chiba, 1978). Marginal inference can be computed in the same cost by backpropagation, if we replace the hard minimum with a soft one in the DTW recursion. This algorithm is known as soft-DTW (Cuturi and Blondel, 2017; Mensch and Blondel, 2018).

Structured SVMs were combined with DTW to learn to predict music-to-score alignments (Garreau et al., 2014). Our framework easily enables extensions of this work, such as replacing DTW with soft-DTW, which amounts to introducing entropic regularization w.r.t. the probability distribution over alignments.

Spanning trees.

When 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}} is the set of possible directed spanning trees (arborescences) of a complete graph 𝒢\mathcal{G} with nn vertices, the convex hull 𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)⊂ℝn⁡(n−1)\conv({\mathcal{Y}})\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n(n-1)} is known as the arborescence polytope (Martins et al., 2009b) (each 𝒚∈𝒴{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}} is a binary vector which indicates which arcs belong to the arborescence). MAP inference may be performed by maximal arborescence algorithms (Chu and Liu, 1965; Edmonds, 1967) in O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) time (Tarjan, 1977), and the Matrix-Tree theorem (Kirchhoff, 1847) provides an O⁡(n3)O(n^{3}) marginal inference algorithm (Koo et al., 2007; Smith and Smith, 2007). Spanning tree structures are often used in natural language processing for (non-projective) dependency parsing, with graph edges corresponding to dependencies between the words in a sentence. (McDonald et al., 2005; Kiperwasser and Goldberg, 2016).

Permutations.

We view ranking as a structured prediction problem. Let 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}} be the set of dd-permutations of a prescribed vector 𝒘∈ℝd{\bm{w}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, i.e., 𝒴={[wπ1,…,wπd]∈ℝd:𝝅∈Π}{\mathcal{Y}}=\{[w_{\pi_{1}},\dots,w_{\pi_{d}}]\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\colon\bm{\pi}\in\Pi\}, where Π\Pi denotes the permutations of (1,…,d)(1,\dots,d). We assume without loss of generality that 𝒘{\bm{w}} is sorted in descending order, i.e., w1≥⋯≥wdw_{1}\geq\dots\geq w_{d}. MAP inference seeks the permutation of 𝒘{\bm{w}} whose inner product with 𝜽\bm{\theta} is maximized:

max𝒚∈𝒴⁡⟨𝜽,𝒚⟩=max⁡∑i=1d𝒚∈𝒴⁡θi​yi=max⁡∑i=1d𝝅∈Π⁡θi​wπi=max⁡∑i=1d𝝅∈Π⁡θπi​wi.\max_{\bm{y}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}{\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{y}}\rangle}=\max_{\bm{y}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\theta_{i}y_{i}=\max_{\bm{\pi}\in\Pi}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\theta_{i}w_{\pi_{i}}=\max_{\bm{\pi}\in\Pi}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\theta_{\pi_{i}}w_{i}. (91)

Since 𝒘{\bm{w}} is assumed sorted, an optimal solution 𝝅⋆\bm{\pi}^{\star} of the last optimization problem is a permutation sorting 𝜽\bm{\theta} in descending order. The function 𝜽↦∑i=1dθπi⋆​wi\bm{\theta}\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^{d}\theta_{\pi^{\star}_{i}}w_{i} is called ordered weighted averaging (OWA) operator (Yager, 1988) and includes the mean and max operator as special cases. MAP inference over 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}} can be seen as the variational formulation of the OWA operator. An optimal solution 𝒚⋆{\bm{y}}^{\star} is simply 𝒘{\bm{w}} sorted using the inverse permutation of 𝝅⋆\bm{\pi}^{\star}. The overall computational cost is therefore O⁡(d​log⁡d)O(d\log d), for sorting 𝜽\bm{\theta}.

The convex hull of 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}}, 𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)\conv({\mathcal{Y}}), is known as the permutahedron when 𝒘=[d,…,1]{\bm{w}}=[d,\dots,1]. For arbitrary 𝒘{\bm{w}}, we follow Lim and Wright (2016) and call 𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)\conv({\mathcal{Y}}) the permutahedron induced by 𝒘{\bm{w}}. Its vertices correspond to permutations of 𝒘{\bm{w}}.

We can define mean-regularized ranking prediction functions 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) if we choose 𝒘{\bm{w}} such that each wiw_{i} represents the “preference” of being in position ii. Intuitively, the score vector 𝜽∈ℝd\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} should be such that each θi\theta_{i} is the score of instance ii (e.g., a document or a label). We give several examples below.

  • •

    Choosing 𝒘=[1,0,…,0]{\bm{w}}=[1,0,\dots,0], 𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)\conv({\mathcal{Y}}) is equal to △d\triangle^{d}, the probability simplex. We thus recover probabilistic classification as a natural special case.

  • •

    Choosing 𝒘=1k[1,…,1⏟k times,0,…,0]{\bm{w}}=\frac{1}{k}[\underbrace{1,\dots,1}_{k\text{ times}},0,\dots,0], 𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)\conv({\mathcal{Y}}) is equal to {𝒑∈△d:‖𝒑‖∞≤1k}\{{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d}\colon\|{\bm{p}}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{1}{k}\}, sometimes referred to as the capped probability simplex (Warmuth and Kuzmin, 2008; Lim and Wright, 2016). This setting corresponds to predicting kk-subsets.

  • •

    Choosing 𝒘=2d⁡(d+1)​[d,d−1,…,1]{\bm{w}}=\frac{2}{d(d+1)}[d,d-1,\dots,1] corresponds to predicting full rankings.

  • •

    Choosing 𝒘=2k⁡(k+1)​[k,k−1,…,1,0,…,0⏟d−k−1​ times]{\bm{w}}=\frac{2}{k(k+1)}[k,k-1,\dots,1,\underbrace{0,\dots,0}_{d-k-1\text{ times}}] corresponds to predicting partial rankings.

The corresponding polytopes are illustrated in Figure 6. In all the examples above, 𝒘∈△d{\bm{w}}\in\triangle^{d}, implying 𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)⊆△d\conv({\mathcal{Y}})\subseteq\triangle^{d}. Therefore, 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) outputs a probability distribution.

As discussed in §3.2, computing the regularized prediction function 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) is equivalent to a Bregman projection when Ω=Ψ+I𝒞\Omega=\Psi+I_{\mathcal{C}}, where Ψ\Psi is Legendre type. The Euclidean projection onto 𝒞=𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴){\mathcal{C}}=\conv({\mathcal{Y}}) reduces to isotonic regression (Zeng and Figueiredo, 2015; Negrinho and Martins, 2014). The computational cost is O⁡(d​log⁡d)O(d\log d). More generally, Bregman projections reduce to isotonic optimization (Lim and Wright, 2016). This provides a unified way to compute 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) efficiently, regardless of 𝒘{\bm{w}}.

The generated Fenchel-Young loss LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}}), is illustrated in Figure 7 for various choices of Ω\Omega. When Ω=0\Omega=0, as expected, the loss is zero as long as the predicted ranking is correct. Note that in order to define a meaningful loss, it is necessary that 𝒚∈𝒴{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}} or more generally 𝒚∈𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴){\bm{y}}\in\conv({\mathcal{Y}}). That is, 𝒚{\bm{y}} should belong to the convex hull of the permutations of 𝒘{\bm{w}}.

Permutahedra have been used to derive online learning to rank algorithms (Yasutake et al., 2011; Ailon et al., 2016) but it is not obvious how to extract a loss from these works. Ordered weighted averaging (OWA) operators have been used to define related top-kk multiclass losses (Usunier et al., 2009; Lapin et al., 2015) but without identifying the connection with permutahedra. Our construction follows directly from the general Fenchel-Young loss framework and provides a novel geometric perspective.

Permutation matrices.

Let 𝒴⊂{0,1}n×n{\mathcal{Y}}\subset\{0,1\}^{n\times n} be the set of n×nn\times n permutation matrices. MAP inference is the solution of the linear assignment problem

max𝒚∈𝒴⁡⟨𝜽,𝒚⟩=max⁡∑i=1n𝝅∈Π⁡θi,πi,\max_{\bm{y}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}{\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{y}}\rangle}=\max_{\bm{\pi}\in\Pi}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\theta_{i,\pi_{i}}, (92)

where Π\Pi denotes the permutations of (1,…,n)(1,\dots,n). The problem can be solved exactly in O⁡(n3)O(n^{3}) time using the Hungarian algorithm (Kuhn, 1955) or the Jonker-Volgenant algorithm (Jonker and Volgenant, 1987). Noticeably, marginal inference is known to be #P-complete (Valiant, 1979; Taskar, 2004, Section 3.5). This makes it an open problem how to solve marginal inference for this polytope.

In contrast, projections on the convex hull of 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}}, the set of doubly stochastic matrices known as Birkhoff polytope (Birkhoff, 1946), can be computed efficiently. Since the Birkhoff polytope is a special case of transportation polytope, we can leverage algorithms from the optimal transport literature to compute the mean-regularized prediction function. When Ω⁡(𝝁)=⟨𝝁,log⁡𝝁⟩\Omega(\bm{\mu})={\langle\bm{\mu},\log\bm{\mu}\rangle}, 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) can be computed using the Sinkhorn algorithm (Sinkhorn and Knopp, 1967; Cuturi, 2013). For other regularizers, we can use Dykstra’s algorithm (Dessein et al., 2016) or dual approaches (Blondel et al., 2018). The cost of obtaining an ϵ\epsilon-approximate solution is typically O⁡(n2/ϵ)O(n^{2}/\epsilon).

The Birkhoff polytope has been used to define continuous relaxations of non-convex ranking losses (Adams and Zemel, 2011). In contrast, the Fenchel-Young loss over the Birkhoff polytope (new to our knowledge) is convex by construction. Although working with permutation matrices is more computationally expensive than working with permutations, it brings different modeling power, since it allows to take into account similarity between instances (e.g., text documents) through the similarity matrix 𝜽\bm{\theta}. It also enables other applications, such as learning to match.

7.4 Structured separation margins

We end this section by extending some of the results in §5 for the structured prediction case, showing that there is also a relation between structured entropies and margins. In the sequel, we assume that structured outputs are contained in a sphere of radius rr, i.e., ‖𝒚‖=r\|{\bm{y}}\|=r for any 𝒚∈𝒴{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}. This holds for all the examples above (sequences, alignments, spanning trees, permutations of a given vector, and permutation matrices). In particular, it holds whenever outputs are represented as binary vectors with a constant number of entries set to 1; this includes overcomplete parametrizations of discrete graphical models (Wainwright and Jordan, 2008).

Definition 12.

Structured separation margin

Let L⁡(𝛉,𝐲)L(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}}) be a loss function over ℝd×𝒴{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\times{\mathcal{Y}}. We say that LL has the structured separation margin property if there exists m>0m>0 such that, for any 𝐲∈𝒴{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}:

⟨𝜽,𝒚⟩≥max𝒚′∈𝒴⁡(⟨𝜽,𝒚′⟩+m2​‖𝒚−𝒚′‖2)⇒L⁡(𝜽,𝒚)=0.{\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{y}}\rangle}\geq\max_{{\bm{y}}^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}\left({\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{y}}^{\prime}\rangle}+\frac{m}{2}\|{\bm{y}}-{\bm{y}}^{\prime}\|^{2}\right)\quad\Rightarrow\quad L(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=0. (93)

The smallest possible mm that satisfies (93) is called the margin of LL, denoted margin⁡(L)\mathrm{margin}(L).

Note that this definition generalizes the unstructured case (Definition 8), which is recovered when 𝒴={𝒆i}i=1d{\mathcal{Y}}=\{\bm{e}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{d}. Note also that, when outputs are represented as binary vectors, the term ‖𝒚−𝒚′‖2\|{\bm{y}}-{\bm{y}}^{\prime}\|^{2} is a Hamming distance, which counts how many bits need to be flipped to transform 𝒚′{\bm{y}}^{\prime} into 𝒚{\bm{y}}. The most famous example of a loss with a structured separation margin in the structured hinge loss used in structured support vector machines (Taskar, 2004; Tsochantaridis et al., 2005).

The next proposition extends Proposition 9. We defer its proof to §B.7.

Proposition 13.

Assume Ω\Omega is convex and 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}} is contained in a sphere of radius rr. Then:

  1. 1.

    The loss LΩL_{\Omega} has a structured separation margin iff there is a m>0m>0 such that, for any 𝒚∈𝒴{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}, m​𝒚∈∂Ω⁡(𝒚)m{\bm{y}}\in\partial\Omega({\bm{y}}).

  2. 2.

    If the above holds, then the margin of LΩL_{\Omega} is given by the smallest such mm or, equivalently,

    margin⁡(LΩ)=sup𝝁∈𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴),𝐲∈𝒴Ω⁡(𝒚)−Ω⁡(𝝁)r2−⟨𝒚,𝝁⟩.\mathrm{margin}(L_{\Omega})=\sup_{\bm{\mu}\in\conv({\mathcal{Y}}),\,{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}\frac{\Omega({\bm{y}})-\Omega(\bm{\mu})}{r^{2}-{\langle{\bm{y}},\bm{\mu}\rangle}}. (94)

Unit margin of the SparseMAP loss.

We can invoke Proposition 13 to show that the SparseMAP loss of Niculae et al. (2018) has a structured margin of 11, a novel result that follows directly from our construction. Indeed, from (94), we have that, for Ω⁡(𝝁)=12​‖𝝁‖2\Omega(\bm{\mu})=\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{\mu}\|^{2}:

margin⁡(LΩ)=sup𝝁∈𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴),𝐲∈𝒴12​r2−12​‖𝝁‖2r2−⟨𝒚,𝝁⟩=1−inf𝝁∈𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴),𝐲∈𝒴12​‖𝒚−𝝁‖2⟨𝒚,𝒚−𝝁⟩≤1,\mathrm{margin}(L_{\Omega})=\sup_{\bm{\mu}\in\conv({\mathcal{Y}}),\,{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}\frac{\frac{1}{2}r^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{\mu}\|^{2}}{r^{2}-{\langle{\bm{y}},\bm{\mu}\rangle}}=1-\inf_{\bm{\mu}\in\conv({\mathcal{Y}}),\,{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}\frac{\frac{1}{2}\|{\bm{y}}-\bm{\mu}\|^{2}}{{\langle{\bm{y}},{\bm{y}}-\bm{\mu}\rangle}}\leq 1, (95)

where the last inequality follows from the fact that both the numerator and denominator in the second term are non-negative, the latter due to the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality. We now show that, for any 𝒚∈𝒴{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}, we have inf𝝁∈𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)12​‖𝒚−𝝁‖2⟨𝒚,𝒚−𝝁⟩=0\inf_{\bm{\mu}\in\conv({\mathcal{Y}})}\frac{\frac{1}{2}\|{\bm{y}}-\bm{\mu}\|^{2}}{{\langle{\bm{y}},{\bm{y}}-\bm{\mu}\rangle}}=0. Choosing 𝝁=t​𝒚′+(1−t)​𝒚\bm{\mu}=t{\bm{y}}^{\prime}+(1-t){\bm{y}}, for an arbitrary 𝒚′∈𝒴∖{𝒚}{\bm{y}}^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{Y}}\setminus\{{\bm{y}}\}, and letting t→0+t\rightarrow 0^{+}, we obtain 12​‖𝒚−𝝁‖2⟨𝒚,𝒚−𝝁⟩=12​t​‖𝒚−𝒚′‖2⟨𝒚,𝒚−𝒚′⟩→0\frac{\frac{1}{2}\|{\bm{y}}-\bm{\mu}\|^{2}}{{\langle{\bm{y}},{\bm{y}}-\bm{\mu}\rangle}}=\frac{\frac{1}{2}t\|{\bm{y}}-{\bm{y}}^{\prime}\|^{2}}{{\langle{\bm{y}},{\bm{y}}-{\bm{y}}^{\prime}\rangle}}\rightarrow 0.

8 Algorithms for learning with Fenchel-Young losses

In this section, we present generic primal (§8.1) and dual (§8.2) algorithms for training predictive models with a Fenchel-Young loss LΩL_{\Omega} for arbitrary Ω\Omega. In doing so, we obtain unified algorithms for training models with a wealth of existing and new loss functions. We then discuss algorithms for computing regularized prediction functions (§8.3) and proximity operators (§8.4). We summarize these “computational oracles” in Figure 8.

8.1 Primal training

Let 𝒇W:𝒳→ℝd\bm{f}_{W}:{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}^{d} be a model parametrized by WW. To learn WW from training data {(𝒙i,𝒚i)}i=1n\{({\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{y}}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}, (𝒙i,𝒚i)∈𝒳×𝒴({\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{y}}_{i})\in{\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}}, we minimize the regularized empirical risk

minW⁡F⁡(W)+G⁡(W)≔∑i=1nLΩ​(𝒇W​(𝒙i),𝒚i)+G⁡(W),\min_{W}F(W)+G(W)\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{n}L_{\Omega}(\bm{f}_{W}({\bm{x}}_{i});{\bm{y}}_{i})+G(W), (96)

where GG is a regularization function w.r.t. parameters WW. Typical examples are Tikhonov regularization, G⁡(W)=λ2​‖W‖F2G(W)=\frac{\lambda}{2}\|W\|_{F}^{2}, and elastic net regularization, G⁡(W)=λ2​‖W‖F2+λ​ρ​‖W‖2G(W)=\frac{\lambda}{2}\|W\|^{2}_{F}+\lambda\rho\|W\|^{2}, for some λ>0\lambda>0 and ρ≥0\rho\geq 0.

The objective in (96) is very broad and allows to learn, e.g., linear models or neural networks using Fenchel-Young losses. Since LΩL_{\Omega} is convex, if 𝒇W\bm{f}_{W} is a linear model and GG is convex, then (96) is convex as well. Assuming further that Ω\Omega is strongly convex, then LΩL_{\Omega} is smooth and (96) can be solved globally using proximal gradient algorithms (Wright et al., 2009; Beck and Teboulle, 2009; Defazio et al., 2014). From Proposition 4, the gradient of LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}}) w.r.t. 𝜽\bm{\theta} is the residual vector

∇LΩ​(𝜽,𝒚)=𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)−𝒚∈ℝd.\nabla L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})-{\bm{y}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}. (97)

Using the chain rule, the gradient of FF w.r.t. WW is

∇F(W)=∑i=1nD𝒇W​(𝒙i)⊤∇LΩ(𝒇W(𝒙i);𝒚i),\nabla F(W)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}D^{\top}_{\bm{f}_{W}({\bm{x}}_{i})}\nabla L_{\Omega}(\bm{f}_{W}({\bm{x}}_{i});{\bm{y}}_{i}), (98)

where D𝒇W​(𝒙i)D_{\bm{f}_{W}({\bm{x}}_{i})} is the Jacobian of 𝒇W​(𝒙i)\bm{f}_{W}({\bm{x}}_{i}) w.r.t. WW, a linear map from the space of WW to ℝd{\mathbb{R}}^{d}. For linear models, we set 𝜽i=𝒇W​(𝒙i)=W​𝒙i\bm{\theta}_{i}=\bm{f}_{W}({\bm{x}}_{i})=W{\bm{x}}_{i}, where W∈ℝd×pW\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d\times p} and 𝒙i∈ℝp{\bm{x}}_{i}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{p}, and thus get

∇F​(W)=(Y^Ω−Y)⊤​X,\nabla F(W)=(\widehat{Y}_{\Omega}-Y)^{\top}X, (99)

where Y^Ω\widehat{Y}_{\Omega}, YY and XX are matrices whose rows gather 𝒚^Ω​(W​𝒙i)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(W{\bm{x}}_{i}), 𝒚i{\bm{y}}_{i} and 𝒙i{\bm{x}}_{i}, for i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n.

In summary, the two main computational ingredients to solve (96) are 𝒚^Ω\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega} and the proximity operator of GG (when GG is non-differentiable). This separation of concerns results in very modular implementations.

Remark on temperature scaling.

When 𝒇W\bm{f}_{W} is a linear model and GG is a homogeneous function, it is easy to check that the temperature scaling parameter t>0t>0 from Proposition 4 and the regularization strength λ>0\lambda>0 above are redundant. Hence, we can set t=1t=1 at training time, without loss of generality. However, at test time, using 𝒚^t​Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{t\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) and tuning tt can potentially improve accuracy. For sparse prediction functions, tt also gives control over sparsity (the smaller, the sparser).

8.2 Dual training

We now derive dual training of Fenchel-Young losses. Although our treatment follows closely Shalev-Shwartz and Zhang (2016), it is different in that we put the output regularization Ω\Omega at the center of all computations, leading to a new perspective.

Dual objective.

For linear models 𝒇W​(𝒙)=W​𝒙\bm{f}_{W}({\bm{x}})=W{\bm{x}}, where W∈ℝd×pW\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d\times p}, it can sometimes be more computationally efficient to solve the corresponding dual problem, especially in the n≪pn\ll p setting. From Fenchel’s duality theorem (see for instance Borwein and Lewis (2010, Theorem 3.3.5)), we find that the dual problem of (96) is

maxα∈ℝn×d−∑i=1nLΩ∗​(−𝜶i,𝒚i)−G∗​(α⊤​X),\max_{\alpha\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n\times d}}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}L_{\Omega}^{*}(-\bm{\alpha}_{i};{\bm{y}}_{i})-G^{*}\left(\alpha^{\top}X\right), (100)

and where LΩ∗L_{\Omega}^{*} is the convex conjugate of LΩL_{\Omega} in its first argument.

We now rewrite the dual problem using the specific form of LΩL_{\Omega}. Using LΩ∗​(−𝜶,𝒚)=Ω⁡(𝒚−𝜶)−Ω⁡(𝒚)L_{\Omega}^{*}(-\bm{\alpha};{\bm{y}})=\Omega({\bm{y}}-\bm{\alpha})-\Omega({\bm{y}}) and using the change of variable 𝝁i≔𝒚i−𝜶i\bm{\mu}_{i}\coloneqq{\bm{y}}_{i}-\bm{\alpha}_{i}, we get

maxμ∈ℝn×d−D⁡(μ)​ s.t. ​𝝁i∈𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)​∀i∈[n],\max_{\mu\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n\times d}}-D(\mu)\text{ s.t. }\bm{\mu}_{i}\in\dom(\Omega)~\forall i\in[n], (101)

where we defined

D⁡(μ)≔∑i=1nΩ⁡(𝝁i)−Ω⁡(𝒚i)+G∗​(V⁡(μ))andV⁡(μ)≔(Y−μ)⊤​X.D(\mu)\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Omega(\bm{\mu}_{i})-\Omega({\bm{y}}_{i})+G^{*}(V(\mu))\quad\text{and}\quad V(\mu)\coloneqq(Y-\mu)^{\top}X. (102)

This expression is informative as we can interpret each 𝝁i\bm{\mu}_{i} as regularized predictions, i.e., 𝝁i\bm{\mu}_{i} should belong to 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)\dom(\Omega), the same domain as 𝒚^Ω\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}. The fact that G∗​(V​(μ))G^{*}(V(\mu)) is a function of the predictions μ\mu is similar to the value regularization framework of Rifkin and Lippert (2007). A key difference with the regularization Ω\Omega, however, is that G∗​(V​(μ))G^{*}(V(\mu)) depends on the training data XX through V⁡(μ)V(\mu). When G⁡(W)=λ2​‖W‖F2⇔G∗​(V)=12​λ​‖V‖F2G(W)=\frac{\lambda}{2}\|W\|^{2}_{F}\Leftrightarrow G^{*}(V)=\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|V\|^{2}_{F}, we obtain G∗​(V⁡(μ))=12​λ​Trace​((Y−μ)⊤​K​(Y−μ))G^{*}(V(\mu))=\frac{1}{2\lambda}\text{Trace}((Y-\mu)^{\top}K(Y-\mu)), where K≔X​X⊤K\coloneqq XX^{\top} is the Gram matrix.

Primal-dual relationship.

Assuming GG is a λ\lambda-strongly convex regularizer, given an optimal dual solution μ⋆\mu^{\star} to (101), we may retrieve the optimal primal solution W⋆W^{\star} by

W⋆=∇G∗​(V⁡(μ⋆)).W^{\star}=\nabla G^{*}(V(\mu^{\star})). (103)

Coordinate ascent.

We can solve (101) using block coordinate ascent algorithms. At every iteration, we pick i∈[n]i\in[n] and consider the following sub-problem associated with ii:

𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝗂𝗇𝝁i∈𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)Ω​(𝝁i)+G∗​(V⁡(μ)).\argmin_{\bm{\mu}_{i}\in\dom(\Omega)}\Omega(\bm{\mu}_{i})+G^{*}(V(\mu)). (104)

Since this problem could be hard to solve, we follow Shalev-Shwartz and Zhang (2016, Option I) and consider instead a quadratic upper-bound. If GG is λ\lambda-strongly convex, G∗G^{*} is 1λ\frac{1}{\lambda}-smooth w.r.t. the dual norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| and it holds that

G∗​(V⁡(μ))≤G∗​(V⁡(μ¯))+⟨∇G∗​(V⁡(μ¯)),V⁡(μ)−V⁡(μ¯)⟩+12​λ​‖V⁡(μ)−V⁡(μ¯)‖2,G^{*}(V(\mu))\leq G^{*}(V(\bar{\mu}))+\langle\nabla G^{*}(V(\bar{\mu})),V(\mu)-V(\bar{\mu})\rangle+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|V(\mu)-V(\bar{\mu})\|^{2}, (105)

where μ¯\bar{\mu} denotes the current iterate of μ\mu. Using V⁡(μ)−V⁡(μ¯)=∑i=1n(𝝁¯i−𝝁i)​𝒙i⊤V(\mu)-V(\bar{\mu})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\bar{\bm{\mu}}_{i}-\bm{\mu}_{i}){\bm{x}}_{i}^{\top}, we get

G∗​(V⁡(μ))≤G∗​(V⁡(μ¯))+∑i=1n⟨∇G∗​(V⁡(μ¯))​𝒙i,𝝁¯i−𝝁i⟩+σi2​‖𝝁¯i−𝝁i‖2,G^{*}(V(\mu))\leq G^{*}(V(\bar{\mu}))+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\langle\nabla G^{*}(V(\bar{\mu})){\bm{x}}_{i},\bar{\bm{\mu}}_{i}-\bm{\mu}_{i}\rangle+\frac{\sigma_{i}}{2}\|\bar{\bm{\mu}}_{i}-\bm{\mu}_{i}\|^{2}, (106)

where σi≔‖𝒙i‖2λ\sigma_{i}\coloneqq\frac{\|{\bm{x}}_{i}\|^{2}}{\lambda}. Substituting G∗​(V​(μ))G^{*}(V(\mu)) by the above upper bound into (104) and ignoring constant terms, we get the following approximate sub-problem:

𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝗂𝗇𝝁i∈𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)Ω​(𝝁i)−𝝁i⊤​𝐯i+σi2​‖𝝁i‖2=𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑1σi​Ω​(𝐯iσi),\argmin_{\bm{\mu}_{i}\in\dom(\Omega)}\Omega(\bm{\mu}_{i})-\bm{\mu}_{i}^{\top}\bm{v}_{i}+\frac{\sigma_{i}}{2}\|\bm{\mu}_{i}\|^{2}=\mathsf{prox}_{\frac{1}{\sigma_{i}}\Omega}\left(\frac{\bm{v}_{i}}{\sigma_{i}}\right), (107)

where 𝒗i≔∇G∗​(V⁡(μ¯))​𝒙i+σi​𝝁i¯\bm{v}_{i}\coloneqq\nabla G^{*}(V(\bar{\mu})){\bm{x}}_{i}+\sigma_{i}\bar{\bm{\mu}_{i}}. Note that when G∗G^{*} is a quadratic function, (107) is an optimal solution of (104).

Examples of parameter regularization GG.

We now give examples of G∗​(W)G^{*}(W) and ∇G∗​(W)\nabla G^{*}(W) for two commonly used regularization: squared ℓ2\ell_{2} and elastic-net regularization.

When G⁡(W)=λ2​‖W‖F2G(W)=\frac{\lambda}{2}\|W\|^{2}_{F}, we obtain

G∗​(V)=12​λ​‖V‖F2and∇G∗​(V)=1λ​V.G^{*}(V)=\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|V\|^{2}_{F}\quad\text{and}\quad\nabla G^{*}(V)=\frac{1}{\lambda}V. (108)

When G⁡(W)=λ2​‖W‖F2+λ​ρ​R​(W)G(W)=\frac{\lambda}{2}\|W\|^{2}_{F}+\lambda\rho R(W), for some other regularizer R⁡(W)R(W), we obtain

∇G∗​(V)\displaystyle\nabla G^{*}(V) =𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑W⟨W,V⟩−λ2​‖W‖F2−λ​ρ​R​(W)\displaystyle=\argmax_{W}~\langle W,V\rangle-\frac{\lambda}{2}\|W\|^{2}_{F}-\lambda\rho R(W) (109)
=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝗂𝗇W12​‖W−Vλ‖F2+ρ​R​(W)\displaystyle=\argmin_{W}~\frac{1}{2}\left\|W-\frac{V}{\lambda}\right\|^{2}_{F}+\rho R(W) (110)
=𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑ρ​R​(V/λ).\displaystyle=\mathsf{prox}_{\rho R}(V/\lambda). (111)

The conjugate is equal to G∗​(V)=⟨∇G∗​(V),V⟩−G⁡(∇G∗​(V))G^{*}(V)=\langle\nabla G^{*}(V),V\rangle-G(\nabla G^{*}(V)).

For instance, if we choose R⁡(W)=‖W‖1R(W)=\|W\|_{1}, then G⁡(W)G(W) is the elastic-net regularization and 𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑ρ​R\mathsf{prox}_{\rho R} is the well-known soft-thresholding operator

𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑ρ​R​(V)=sign​(V)​[|V|−ρ]+,\mathsf{prox}_{\rho R}(V)=\text{sign}(V)[|V|-\rho]_{+}, (112)

where all operations above are performed element-wise.

Summary.

To summarize, on each iteration, we pick i∈[n]i\in[n] and perform the update

𝝁i←𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑1σi​Ω​(𝒗i/σi),\bm{\mu}_{i}\leftarrow\mathsf{prox}_{\frac{1}{\sigma_{i}}\Omega}(\bm{v}_{i}/\sigma_{i}), (113)

where we defined 𝒗i≔∇G∗​(V⁡(μ))​𝒙i+σi​𝝁i\bm{v}_{i}\coloneqq\nabla G^{*}(V(\mu)){\bm{x}}_{i}+\sigma_{i}\bm{\mu}_{i} and σi≔‖𝒙i‖2λ\sigma_{i}\coloneqq\frac{\|{\bm{x}}_{i}\|^{2}}{\lambda}. This update does not require choosing any learning rate. Interestingly, if 𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑τ​Ω\mathsf{prox}_{\tau\Omega} is sparse, then so are the dual variables {𝝁i}i=1n\{\bm{\mu}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}. Sparsity in the dual variables is particularly useful when kernelizing models, as it makes computing predictions more efficient.

When ii is picked uniformly at random, this block coordinate ascent algorithm is known to converge to an optimal solution W⋆W^{\star}, at a linear rate if LΩL_{\Omega} is smooth (i.e., if Ω\Omega is strongly convex) (Shalev-Shwartz and Zhang, 2016). When 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)\dom(\Omega) is a compact set, another option to solve (101) that does not involve proximity operators is the block Frank-Wolfe algorithm (Lacoste-Julien et al., 2012).

8.3 Regularized prediction functions

The regularized prediction function 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) does not generally enjoy a closed-form expression and one must resort to generic algorithms to compute it. In this section, we first discuss two such algorithms: projected gradient and conditional gradient methods. Then, we present a new more efficient algorithm when 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)⊆△d\dom(\Omega)\subseteq\triangle^{d} and Ω\Omega is uniformly separable.

Generic algorithms.

In their greater generality, regularized prediction functions involve the following optimization problem

min𝝁∈𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)⁡f𝜽​(𝝁)≔Ω⁡(𝝁)−⟨𝜽,𝝁⟩.\min_{\bm{\mu}\in\dom(\Omega)}f_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\mu})\coloneqq\Omega(\bm{\mu})-{\langle\bm{\theta},\bm{\mu}\rangle}. (114)

Assuming Ω\Omega is convex and smooth (differentiable and with Lipschitz-continuous gradient), we can solve this problem to arbitrary precision using projected gradient methods. Unfortunately, the projection onto 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)\dom(\Omega), which is needed by these algorithms, is often as challenging to solve as (114) itself. This is especially the case when 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)\dom(\Omega) is 𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗏(𝒴)\conv({\mathcal{Y}}), the convex hull of a combinatorial set of structured objects.

Assuming further that 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)\dom(\Omega) is a compact set, an appealing alternative which sidesteps these issues is provided by conditional gradient (a.k.a. Frank-Wolfe) algorithms (Frank and Wolfe, 1956; Dunn and Harshbarger, 1978; Jaggi, 2013). Their main advantage stems from the fact that they access 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)\dom(\Omega) only through the linear maximization oracle
𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑𝐲∈𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)⟨𝜽,𝐲⟩\argmax_{{\bm{y}}\in\dom(\Omega)}{\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{y}}\rangle}. CG algorithms maintain the current solution as a sparse convex combination of vertices of 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω)\dom(\Omega). At each iteration, the linear maximization oracle is used to pick a new vertex to add to the combination. Despite its simplicity, the procedure converges to an optimal solution, albeit at a sub-linear rate (Jaggi, 2013). Linear convergence rates can be obtained using away-step, pairwise and full-corrective variants (Lacoste-Julien and Jaggi, 2015). When Ω\Omega is a quadratic function (as in the case of SparseMAP), an approximate correction step can achieve finite convergence efficiently. The resulting algorithm is known as the active set method (Nocedal and Wright, 1999, chapters 16.4 & 16.5), and is a generalization of Wolfe’s min-norm point algorithm (Wolfe, 1976). See also Vinyes and Obozinski (2017) for a more detailed discussion on these algorithms and Niculae et al. (2018) for an instantiation, in the specific case of SparseMAP.

Although not explored in this paper, similar algorithms have been developed to minimize a function over conic hulls (Locatello et al., 2017). Such algorithms allow to compute a regularized prediction function that outputs a conic combination of elementary structures, instead of a convex one. It can be seen as the structured counterpart of the regularized prediction function over positive measures (§6).

Reduction to root finding.

When Ω\Omega is a strictly convex regularization function over △d\triangle^{d} and is uniformly separable, i.e., Ω⁡(𝒑)=∑i=1dg⁡(pi)\Omega({\bm{p}})=\sum_{i=1}^{d}g(p_{i}) for some strictly convex function gg, we now show that 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}) can be computed in linear time.

Proposition 14.

Reduction to root finding

Let g:[0,1]→ℝ+g\colon[0,1]\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}_{+} be a strictly convex and differentiable function. Then,

𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝖺𝗑𝐩∈△d⟨𝐩,𝜽⟩−∑j=1dg⁡(pj)=𝐩⁡(τ⋆)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta})=\argmax_{{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d}}{\langle{\bm{p}},\bm{\theta}\rangle}-\sum_{j=1}^{d}g(p_{j})={\bm{p}}(\tau^{\star})

where

𝒑⁡(τ)≔(g′)−1​(max⁡{𝜽−τ,g′​(0)}){\bm{p}}(\tau)\coloneqq(g^{\prime})^{-1}(\max\{\bm{\theta}-\tau,g^{\prime}(0)\})\quad (115)

and where τ⋆\tau^{\star} is a root of ϕ⁡(τ)≔⟨𝐩⁡(τ),𝟏⟩−1\phi(\tau)\coloneqq{\langle{\bm{p}}(\tau),\bm{1}\rangle}-1.

Moreover, τ⋆\tau^{\star} belongs to the tight search interval [τmin,τmax][\tau_{\min},\tau_{\max}], where

τmin≔max⁡(𝜽)−g′​(1)andτmax≔max⁡(𝜽)−g′​(1/d).\tau_{\min}\coloneqq\max(\bm{\theta})-g^{\prime}(1)\quad\text{and}\quad\tau_{\max}\coloneqq\max(\bm{\theta})-g^{\prime}\left(\nicefrac{{1}}{{d}}\right). (116)

The equation of 𝒑⁡(τ){\bm{p}}(\tau) can be seen as a generalization of (12). An approximate τ\tau such that |ϕ⁡(τ)|≤ϵ|\phi(\tau)|\leq\epsilon can be found in O⁡(1/log⁡ϵ)O(\nicefrac{{1}}{{\log\epsilon}}) time by, e.g., bisection. The related problem of Bregman projection onto the probability simplex was recently studied by Krichene et al. (2015) but our derivation is different and more direct (cf. §B.8).

For example, when Ω\Omega is the negative α\alpha-Tsallis entropy −𝖧αt-\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{t}}_{\alpha}, which we saw can be written in separable form in (52), we obtain

g(t)=tα−tα⁡(α−1),g′(t)=tα−1−1α−1and(g′)−1(s)=(1+(α−1)s)1α−1,g(t)=\frac{t^{\alpha}-t}{\alpha(\alpha-1)},\quad g^{\prime}(t)=\frac{t^{\alpha-1}-1}{\alpha-1}\quad\text{and}\quad(g^{\prime})^{-1}(s)=\big(1+(\alpha-1)s\big)^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}},

yielding

𝒑⁡(τ)=(1+(α−1)​max⁡(𝜽−τ,−1/α−1))1α−1.{\bm{p}}(\tau)=\big(1+(\alpha-1)\max(\bm{\theta}-\tau,\nicefrac{{-1}}{{\alpha-1}})\big)^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}}.

From the root τ⋆\tau^{\star} of ϕ⁡(τ)=⟨𝒑⁡(τ),𝟏⟩−1\phi(\tau)={\langle{\bm{p}}(\tau),\bm{1}\rangle}-1, we obtain 𝒚^−𝖧αt​(𝜽)=𝒑⁡(τ⋆)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{-\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{t}}_{\alpha}}(\bm{\theta})={\bm{p}}(\tau^{\star}).

8.4 Proximity operators

Computing the proximity operator 𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑τ​Ω​(𝜼)\mathsf{prox}_{\tau\Omega}(\bm{\eta}), defined in (2), usually involves a more challenging optimization problem than 𝒚^Ω​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}). For instance, when Ω\Omega is Shannon’s negative entropy over △d\triangle^{d}, 𝒚^Ω\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega} enjoys a closed-form solution (the softmax) but not 𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑Ω\mathsf{prox}_{\Omega}. However, we can always compute 𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑τ​Ω​(𝜼)\mathsf{prox}_{\tau\Omega}(\bm{\eta}) by first-order gradient methods given access to 𝒚^Ω\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}. Indeed, using the Moreau decomposition, we have

𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑τ​Ω​(𝜼)=𝜼−𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑Ω∗τ​(𝜼/τ).\mathsf{prox}_{\tau\Omega}(\bm{\eta})=\bm{\eta}-\mathsf{prox}_{\frac{\Omega^{*}}{\tau}}(\bm{\eta}/\tau). (117)

Since 𝖽𝗈𝗆(Ω∗)=ℝd\dom(\Omega^{*})={\mathbb{R}}^{d}, computing 𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑Ω∗τ​(𝜼/τ)\mathsf{prox}_{\frac{\Omega^{*}}{\tau}}(\bm{\eta}/\tau) only involves an unconstrained optimization problem, 𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝗂𝗇𝜽∈ℝd12​‖𝜽−𝜼/τ‖2+1τ​Ω∗​(𝜽)\argmin_{\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{\theta}-\bm{\eta}/\tau\|^{2}+\frac{1}{\tau}\Omega^{*}(\bm{\theta}). Since ∇Ω∗=𝒚^Ω\nabla\Omega^{*}=\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}, that optimization problem can easily be solved by any first-order gradient method given access to 𝒚^Ω\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}. For specific choices of Ω\Omega, 𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑τ​Ω​(𝜼)\mathsf{prox}_{\tau\Omega}(\bm{\eta}) can be computed directly more efficiently, as we now discuss.

Closed-form expressions.

We now give examples of commonly-used loss functions for which 𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑τ​Ω\mathsf{prox}_{\tau\Omega} enjoys a closed-form expression.

For the squared loss, we choose Ω⁡(𝝁)=12​‖𝝁‖2\Omega(\bm{\mu})=\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{\mu}\|^{2}. Hence:

𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑τ​Ω​(𝜼)=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝗂𝗇𝝁∈ℝd12​‖𝝁−𝜼‖2+τ2​‖𝝁‖2=𝜼τ+1.\mathsf{prox}_{\tau\Omega}(\bm{\eta})=\argmin_{\bm{\mu}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{\mu}-\bm{\eta}\|^{2}+\frac{\tau}{2}\|\bm{\mu}\|^{2}=\frac{\bm{\eta}}{\tau+1}. (118)

For the perceptron loss (Rosenblatt, 1958; Collins, 2002), we choose Ω=I△d\Omega=I_{\triangle^{d}}. Hence:

𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑τ​Ω​(𝜼)=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝗂𝗇𝐩∈△d12​‖𝐩−𝜼‖2.\mathsf{prox}_{\tau\Omega}(\bm{\eta})=\argmin_{{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d}}\frac{1}{2}\|{\bm{p}}-\bm{\eta}\|^{2}. (119)

For the sparsemax loss (Martins and Astudillo, 2016), we choose Ω=12∥⋅∥2+I△d\Omega=\frac{1}{2}\|\cdot\|^{2}+I_{\triangle^{d}}. Hence:

𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑τ​Ω​(𝜼)=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝗂𝗇𝐩∈△d12​‖𝐩−𝜼‖2+τ2​‖𝐩‖2=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝗂𝗇𝐩∈△d12​‖𝐩−𝜼τ+1‖2.\mathsf{prox}_{\tau\Omega}(\bm{\eta})=\argmin_{{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d}}\frac{1}{2}\|{\bm{p}}-\bm{\eta}\|^{2}+\frac{\tau}{2}\|{\bm{p}}\|^{2}=\argmin_{{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d}}\frac{1}{2}\left\|{\bm{p}}-\frac{\bm{\eta}}{\tau+1}\right\|^{2}. (120)

For the cost-sensitive multiclass hinge loss, we choose Ω=I△d−⟨⋅,𝒄𝒚⟩\Omega=I_{\triangle^{d}}-\langle\cdot,\bm{c}_{{\bm{y}}}\rangle. Hence:

𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑τ​Ω​(𝜼)=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝗂𝗇𝐩∈△d12​‖𝐩−𝜼‖2−τ⁡⟨𝐩,𝐜𝐲⟩=𝖺𝗋𝗀𝗆𝗂𝗇𝐩∈△d12​‖𝐩−(𝜼+τ​𝐜𝐲)‖2.\mathsf{prox}_{\tau\Omega}(\bm{\eta})=\argmin_{{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d}}\frac{1}{2}\|{\bm{p}}-\bm{\eta}\|^{2}-\tau\langle{\bm{p}},\bm{c}_{{\bm{y}}}\rangle=\argmin_{{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d}}\frac{1}{2}\|{\bm{p}}-(\bm{\eta}+\tau\bm{c}_{{\bm{y}}})\|^{2}. (121)

Choosing 𝒄𝒚=𝟏−𝒚\bm{c}_{{\bm{y}}}=\bm{1}-{\bm{y}}, where 𝒚∈{𝒆i}i=1d{\bm{y}}\in\{\bm{e}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{d} is the ground-truth label, gives the proximity operator for the usual multiclass hinge loss (Crammer and Singer, 2001).

For the Shannon entropy and 1.51.5-Tsallis entropy, we show that 𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑−𝖧\mathsf{prox}_{-\mathsf{H}} reduces to root finding in Appendix A.1.

9 Experiments

In this section, we demonstrate one of the key features of Fenchel-Young losses: their ability to induce sparse probability distributions. We focus on two tasks: label proportion estimation (§9.1) and dependency parsing (§9.2).

9.1 Label proportion estimation experiments

As we saw in §4, α\alpha-Tsallis entropies generate a family of losses, with the logistic (α→1\alpha\to 1) and sparsemax losses (α=2\alpha=2) as important special cases. In addition, they are twice differentiable for α∈[1,2)\alpha\in[1,2), produce sparse probability distributions for α>1\alpha>1 and are computationally efficient for any α≥1\alpha\geq 1, thanks to Proposition  14. In this section, we demonstrate their effectiveness on the task of label proportion estimation and compare different solvers for computing the regularized prediction function 𝒚^−𝖧αt\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{-\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{t}}_{\alpha}}.

Experimental setup.

Given an input vector 𝒙∈𝒳⊆ℝp{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}}\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}^{p}, where pp is the number of features, our goal is to estimate a vector of label proportions 𝒚∈△d{\bm{y}}\in\triangle^{d}, where dd is the number of classes. If 𝒚{\bm{y}} is sparse, we expect the superiority of Tsallis losses over the conventional logistic loss on this task. At training time, given a set of nn pairs (𝒙i,𝒚i)({\bm{x}}_{i},{\bm{y}}_{i}), we estimate a matrix W∈ℝd×pW\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d\times p} by minimizing the convex objective

R⁡(W)≔∑i=1nLΩ​(W​𝒙i,𝒚i)+λ2​‖W‖F2.R(W)\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{n}L_{\Omega}(W{\bm{x}}_{i};{\bm{y}}_{i})+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|W\|_{F}^{2}. (122)

We optimize the loss using L-BFGS (Liu and Nocedal, 1989). From Proposition 4 and using the chain rule, we obtain the gradient expression ∇R​(W)=(Y^Ω−Y)⊤​X+λ​W\nabla R(W)=(\widehat{Y}_{\Omega}-Y)^{\top}X+\lambda W, where Y^Ω\widehat{Y}_{\Omega}, YY and XX are matrices whose rows gather 𝒚^Ω​(W​𝒙i)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(W{\bm{x}}_{i}), 𝒚i{\bm{y}}_{i} and 𝒙i{\bm{x}}_{i}, for i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n. At test time, we predict label proportions by 𝒑=𝒚^−𝖧αt​(W​𝒙){\bm{p}}=\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{-\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{t}}_{\alpha}}(W{\bm{x}}).

Real data experiments.

We ran experiments on 77 standard multi-label benchmark datasets — see Table 3 for dataset characteristics11 1 The datasets can be downloaded from http://mulan.sourceforge.net/datasets-mlc.html and https://www.csie.ntu.edu.tw/~cjlin/libsvmtools/datasets/.. For all datasets, we removed samples with no label, normalized samples to have zero mean unit variance, and normalized labels to lie in the probability simplex. We chose λ∈{10−4,10−3,…,104}\lambda\in\{10^{-4},10^{-3},\dots,10^{4}\} and α∈{1,1.1,…,2}\alpha\in\{1,1.1,\dots,2\} against the validation set. We report the test set mean Jensen-Shannon divergence, JS(𝒑,𝒚)≔1/2KL(𝒑∥𝒑+𝒚2)+1/2KL(𝒚∥𝒑+𝒚2)\text{JS}({\bm{p}},{\bm{y}})\coloneqq\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}}\operatorname{KL}({\bm{p}}\|\frac{{\bm{p}}+{\bm{y}}}{2})+\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}}\operatorname{KL}({\bm{y}}\|\frac{{\bm{p}}+{\bm{y}}}{2}), and the mean squared error 1/2​‖𝒑−𝒚‖2\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}}\,\|{\bm{p}}-{\bm{y}}\|^{2} in Table 4. As can be seen, the loss with tuned α\alpha achieves the best averaged rank overall. Tuning α\alpha allows to choose the best loss in the family in a data-driven fashion.

Synthetic data experiments.

We follow Martins and Astudillo (2016) and generate a document 𝒙∈ℝp{\bm{x}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{p} from a mixture of multinomials and label proportions 𝒚∈△d{\bm{y}}\in\triangle^{d} from a multinomial. The number of words in 𝒙{\bm{x}} and labels in 𝒚{\bm{y}} is sampled from a Poisson distribution — see Martins and Astudillo (2016) for a precise description of the generative process. We use 1200 samples as training set, 200 samples as validation set and 1000 samples as test set. We tune λ∈{10−6,10−5,…,100}\lambda\in\{10^{-6},10^{-5},\dots,10^{0}\} and α∈{1.0,1.1,…,2.0}\alpha\in\{1.0,1.1,\dots,2.0\} against the validation set. We report the Jensen-Shannon divergence in Figure 10. Results using the mean squared error (MSE) were entirely similar. When the number of classes is 10, Tsallis and sparsemax losses perform almost exactly the same, both outperforming softmax. When the number of classes is 50, Tsallis losses outperform both sparsemax and softmax.

Solver comparison.

We also compared bisection (binary search) and Brent’s method for solving (8) by root finding (Proposition 14). We focus on 𝖧1.5t\mathsf{H}^{\textsc{t}}_{1.5}, i.e. the 1.51.5-Tsallis entropy, and also compare against using a generic projected gradient algorithm (FISTA) to solve (8) naively. We measure the time needed to reach a solution 𝒑{\bm{p}} with ‖𝒑−𝒑⋆‖2<10−5\|{\bm{p}}-{\bm{p}}^{\star}\|_{2}<10^{-5}, over 200 samples 𝜽∈ℝd∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,σ​𝑰)\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},\sigma\bm{I}) with log⁡σ∼𝒰⁡(−4,4)\log\sigma\sim\mathcal{U}(-4,4). Median and 99% CI times reported in Figure 9 reveal that root finding scales better, with Brent’s method outperforming FISTA by one to two orders of magnitude.

9.2 Dependency parsing experiments

We next compare Fenchel-Young losses for structured output prediction, as formulated in §7, for non-projective dependency parsing. The application consists of predicting the directed tree of grammatical dependencies between words in a sentence (Jurafsky and Martin, 2018, Chapter 14). We tackle it by learning structured models over the arborescence polytope, using the structured SVM, CRF, and SparseMAP losses (Niculae et al., 2018), which we saw to all be instances of Fenchel-Young loss. Training data, as in the CoNLL 2017 shared task (Zeman et al., 2017), comes from the Universal Dependency project (Nivre et al., 2016). To isolate the effect of the loss, we use the provided gold tokenization and part-of-speech tags. We follow closely the bidirectional LSTM arc-factored parser of Kiperwasser and Goldberg (2016), using the same model configuration; the only exception is not using externally pretrained embeddings. Parameters are trained using Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015), tuning the learning rate on the grid {.5,1,2,4,8}×10−3\{.5,1,2,4,8\}\times 10^{-3}, expanded by a factor of 2 if the best model is at either end.

We experiment with 5 languages, diverse both in terms of family and in terms of the amount of training data (ranging from 1,400 sentences for Vietnamese to 12,525 for English). Test set results (Table 5) indicate that SparseMAP outperforms the CRF loss and is competitive with the structured SVM loss, outperforming it substantially on Chinese. The Fenchel-Young perspective sheds further light onto the empirical results, as the SparseMAP loss and the structured SVM (unlike the CRF) both enjoy the margin property with margin 1, while both SparseMAP and the CRF loss (unlike structured SVM) are differentiable.

10 Related work

10.1 Loss functions

Proper losses.

Proper losses, a.k.a. proper scoring rules, are a well-studied object in statistics (Grünwald and Dawid (2004); Gneiting and Raftery (2007); references therein) and more recently in machine learning (Reid and Williamson, 2010; Williamson et al., 2016). A loss ℓ⁡(𝒑,𝒚)\ell({\bm{p}};{\bm{y}}), between a ground truth 𝒚∈△d{\bm{y}}\in\triangle^{d} and a probability forecast 𝒑∈△d{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d}, where dd is the number of classes, is said to be proper if it is minimized when estimating the true 𝒚{\bm{y}}. Formally, a proper loss ℓ\ell satisfies

ℓ⁡(𝒚,𝒚)≤ℓ⁡(𝒑,𝒚)∀𝒑,𝒚∈△d.\ell({\bm{y}};{\bm{y}})\leq\ell({\bm{p}};{\bm{y}})\quad\forall{\bm{p}},{\bm{y}}\in\triangle^{d}. (123)

It is strictly proper if the inequality is strict when 𝒑≠𝒚{\bm{p}}\neq{\bm{y}}, implying that it is uniquely minimized by predicting the correct probability. Strictly proper losses induce Fisher consistent estimators of probabilities (Williamson et al., 2016). A key result, which dates back to Savage (1971) (see also Gneiting and Raftery (2007)), is that given a regularization function Ω:△d→ℝ\Omega\colon\triangle^{d}\to{\mathbb{R}}, the function ℓΩ:△d×△d→ℝ+\ell_{\Omega}\colon\triangle^{d}\times\triangle^{d}\to{\mathbb{R}}_{+} defined by

ℓΩ​(𝒑,𝒚)≔⟨∇Ω​(𝒑),𝒚−𝒑⟩−Ω⁡(𝒑)\ell_{\Omega}({\bm{p}};{\bm{y}})\coloneqq\langle\nabla\Omega({\bm{p}}),{\bm{y}}-{\bm{p}}\rangle-\Omega({\bm{p}}) (124)

is proper. It is easy to see that ℓΩ(𝒑;𝒚)=BΩ(𝒚∥𝒑)−Ω(𝒚)\ell_{\Omega}({\bm{p}};{\bm{y}})=B_{\Omega}({\bm{y}}\|{\bm{p}})-\Omega({\bm{y}}), which recovers the well-known Bregman divergence representation of proper losses. For example, using the Gini index 𝖧⁡(𝒑)=1−‖𝒑‖2\mathsf{H}({\bm{p}})=1-\|{\bm{p}}\|^{2} generates the Brier score (Brier, 1950)

ℓ−𝖧(𝒑;𝒆k)=∑i=1d([[k=i]]−pi)2,\ell_{-\mathsf{H}}({\bm{p}};\bm{e}_{k})=\sum_{i=1}^{d}([[k=i]]-p_{i})^{2}, (125)

showing that the sparsemax loss and the Brier score share the same generating function.

More generally, while a proper loss ℓΩ\ell_{\Omega} is related to a primal-space Bregman divergence, a Fenchel-Young loss LΩL_{\Omega} can be seen as a mixed-space Bregman divergence (§3). This difference has a number of important consequences. First, ℓΩ\ell_{\Omega} is not necessarily convex in 𝒑{\bm{p}} (Williamson et al. (2016, Proposition 17) show that it is in fact quasi-convex). In contrast, LΩL_{\Omega} is always convex in 𝜽\bm{\theta}. Second, the first argument is constrained to △d\triangle^{d} for ℓΩ\ell_{\Omega}, while unconstrained for LΩL_{\Omega}.

In practice, proper losses are often composed with an invertible link function 𝝍−1:ℝd→△d\bm{\psi}^{-1}\colon{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\to\triangle^{d}. This form of a loss, ℓΩ​(𝝍−1​(𝜽),𝒚)\ell_{\Omega}(\bm{\psi}^{-1}(\bm{\theta});{\bm{y}}), is sometimes called composite (Buja et al., 2005; Reid and Williamson, 2010; Williamson et al., 2016). However, the composition of ℓΩ​(⋅,𝒚)\ell_{\Omega}(\cdot;{\bm{y}}) and 𝝍−1​(𝜽)\bm{\psi}^{-1}(\bm{\theta}) is not necessarily convex in 𝜽\bm{\theta}. The canonical link function (Buja et al., 2005) of ℓΩ\ell_{\Omega} is a link function that ensures the convexity of ℓΩ​(𝝍−1​(𝜽),𝒚)\ell_{\Omega}(\bm{\psi}^{-1}(\bm{\theta});{\bm{y}}) in 𝜽\bm{\theta}. It also plays a key role in generalized linear models (Nelder and Baker, 1972; McCullagh and Nelder, 1989). Following Proposition 6, when Ω\Omega is Legendre type, we obtain

LΩ(𝜽;𝒚)=BΩ(𝒚∥𝒚^Ω(𝜽))=ℓΩ(𝒚^Ω(𝜽);𝒚)+Ω(𝒚).L_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta};{\bm{y}})=B_{\Omega}({\bm{y}}\|\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta}))=\ell_{\Omega}(\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega}(\bm{\theta});{\bm{y}})+\Omega({\bm{y}}). (126)

Thus, in this case, Fenchel-Young losses and proper composite losses coincide up to the constant term Ω⁡(𝒚)\Omega({\bm{y}}) (which vanishes if 𝒚=𝒆k{\bm{y}}=\bm{e}_{k} and Ω\Omega satisfies assumption A.1), with 𝝍−1=𝒚^Ω\bm{\psi}^{-1}=\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{\Omega} the canonical inverse link function. Fenchel-Young losses, however, require neither invertible link nor Legendre type assumptions, allowing to express losses (e.g., hinge or sparsemax) that are not expressible in composite form. Moreover, as seen in §5, a Legendre-type Ω\Omega precisely precludes sparse probability distributions and losses enjoying a margin. However, the decoupling between loss and link as promoted by proper composite losses also has some merits (Reid and Williamson, 2010). For instance, using a non-canonical link is useful to express the exponential loss of Adaboost (Nowak-Vila et al., 2019).

Other related losses.

Nock and Nielsen (2009) proposed a binary classification loss construction. Technically, their loss is based on the Legendre transformation (a subset of Fenchel conjugate functions), precluding non-invertible mappings. Masnadi-Shirazi (2011) studied the Bayes consistency of related binary classification loss functions. Duchi et al. (2018, Proposition 3) derived the multi-class loss (45), a special case of Fenchel-Young loss over the probability simplex, and showed (Proposition 4) that any strictly concave generalized entropy generates a classification-calibrated loss. Amid and Warmuth (2017) proposed a different family of losses based on the Tsallis divergence, to interpolate between convex and non-convex losses, for robustness to label noise. Finally, several works have explored connections between another divergence, the ff-divergence (Csiszár, 1975), and surrogate loss functions (Nguyen et al., 2009; Reid and Williamson, 2011; Garcia-Garcia and Williamson, 2012; Duchi et al., 2018).

Consistency.

In this paper, we have not addressed the question of the consistency of Fenchel-Young losses when used as a surrogate for a (possibly non-convex) loss. Although consistency has been widely studied in the multiclass setting (Zhang, 2004; Bartlett et al., 2006; Tewari and Bartlett, 2007; Mroueh et al., 2012) and in other specific settings (Duchi et al., 2010; Ravikumar et al., 2011), it is only recently that it was studied for general losses in a fully general structured prediction setting. Since the publication of this paper, sufficient conditions for consistency have been established for composite losses (Nowak-Vila et al., 2019) and for projection-based losses (Blondel, 2019), both a subset of Fenchel-Young losses. As shown in these works, the strong convexity of Ω\Omega plays a crucial role.

10.2 Fenchel duality in machine learning

In this paper, we make extensive use of Fenchel duality to derive loss functions. Fenchel duality has also played a key role in several machine learning studies before. It was used to provide a unifying perspective on convex empirical risk minimization and representer theorems (Rifkin and Lippert, 2007). It was also used for deriving regret bounds (Shalev-Shwartz and Singer, 2007; Shalev-Shwartz and Kakade, 2009), risk bounds (Kakade et al., 2009), and unified analyses of boosting (Shen and Li, 2010; Shalev-Shwartz and Singer, 2010; Telgarsky, 2012). However, none of these works propose loss functions, as we do. More closely related to our work are smoothing techniques (Nesterov, 2005; Beck and Teboulle, 2012), which have been used extensively to create smoothed versions of existing losses (Song et al., 2014; Shalev-Shwartz and Zhang, 2016). However, these techniques were applied on a per-loss basis and were not connected to an induced probability distribution. In contrast, we propose a generic loss construction, with clear links between smoothing / regularization and the probability distribution produced by regularized prediction functions.

10.3 Approximate inference with conditional gradient algorithms

In this paper, we suggest conditional gradient (CG) algorithms as a powerful tool for computing regularized prediction functions and Fenchel-Young losses over potentially complex output domains. CG algorithms have been used before to compute an approximate solution to intractable marginal inference problems (Belanger et al., 2013; Krishnan et al., 2015) or to sample from an intractable distribution so as to approximate its mean (Bach et al., 2012; Lacoste-Julien et al., 2015). When combined with reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS), these ideas are closely related maximum mean discrepancy (Gretton et al., 2012).

11 Conclusion

We showed that the notion of output regularization and Fenchel duality provide simple core principles, unifying many existing loss functions, and allowing to create useful new ones easily, on a large spectrum of tasks. We characterized a tight connection between sparse distributions and losses with a separation margin, and showed that these losses are precisely the ones that cannot be written in proper composite loss form. We established the computational tools to efficiently learn with Fenchel-Young losses, whether in unstructured or structured settings. We expect that this groundwork will enable the creation of many more novel losses in the future, by exploring other convex polytopes and regularizers.

A.2 Loss “Fenchel-Youngization”

Not all loss functions proposed in the literature can be written in Fenchel-Young loss form. In this section, we present a natural method to approximate (in a sense we will clarify) any loss ℓ:ℝd×{𝒆i}i=1d→ℝ+\ell\colon{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\times\{\bm{e}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{d}\to{\mathbb{R}}_{+} with a Fenchel-Young loss. This has two main advantages. First, the resulting loss is convex even when ℓ\ell is not. Second, the associated regularized prediction function can be used for probabilistic prediction even if ℓ\ell is not probabilistic.

From loss to entropy.

Equations (47) and (48), which relate entropy and conditional Bayes risk, suggest a reverse construction from entropy to loss function. This direction has been explored in previous works (Grünwald and Dawid, 2004; Duchi et al., 2018). The entropy 𝖧ℓ\mathsf{H}_{\ell} generated from ℓ\ell is defined as follows:

𝖧ℓ​(𝒑)≔inf𝜽∈ℝd𝔼𝒑​[ℓ⁡(𝜽,Y)]=inf𝜽∈ℝd∑i=1dpi​ℓ​(𝜽,𝒆i).\mathsf{H}_{\ell}({\bm{p}})\coloneqq\inf_{\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}{\mathbb{E}}_{{\bm{p}}}[\ell(\bm{\theta};Y)]=\inf_{\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}p_{i}\ell(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{i}). (138)

This is the infimum of a linear and thus concave function of 𝒑{\bm{p}}. Hence, by Danskin’s theorem (Danskin, 1966; Bertsekas, 1999, Proposition B.25), Hℓ​(𝒑)H_{\ell}({\bm{p}}) is concave (note that this is true even if ℓ\ell is not convex). As an example, Duchi et al. (2018, Example 1) show that the entropy associated with the zero-one loss is 𝖧ℓ​(𝒑)=1−maxj⁡pj\mathsf{H}_{\ell}({\bm{p}})=1-\max_{j}p_{j}. As we discussed in §4.3, this entropy is known as the Berger-Parker dominance index (Berger and Parker, 1970), and is a special case of norm entropy (54).

The following new proposition shows how to compute the entropy of pairwise hinge losses.

Proposition 15.

Entropy generated by pairwise hinge losses

See Appendix B.9 for a proof. The first one recovers (Duchi et al., 2018, Example 5) with a simpler proof. The last two are new. These entropies are illustrated in Figure 11. For the last two choices, 𝖧ℓ\mathsf{H}_{\ell} is strictly concave over △d\triangle^{d} and the associated prediction function 𝒚^−𝖧ℓ​(𝜽)\widehat{{\bm{y}}}_{-\mathsf{H}_{\ell}}(\bm{\theta}) is typically sparse, although we are not aware of a closed-form expression.

And back to Fenchel-Young loss.

A natural idea is then to construct a Fenchel-Young from 𝖧ℓ\mathsf{H}_{\ell}. The resulting loss is convex by construction. Let us assume for simplicity that ℓ\ell achieves its minimum at 00, implying 𝖧ℓ​(𝒆k)=0\mathsf{H}_{\ell}(\bm{e}_{k})=0. Combining (45) and (138), we obtain

L−𝖧ℓ​(𝜽,𝒆k)\displaystyle L_{-\mathsf{H}_{\ell}}(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{k}) =(−𝖧ℓ)∗​(𝜽)−θk\displaystyle=(-\mathsf{H}_{\ell})^{*}(\bm{\theta})-\theta_{k} (139)
=max𝒑∈△d⁡⟨𝜽,𝒑⟩+𝖧ℓ​(𝒑)−θk\displaystyle=\max_{{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d}}{\langle\bm{\theta},{\bm{p}}\rangle}+\mathsf{H}_{\ell}({\bm{p}})-\theta_{k} (140)
=max𝒑∈△d⁡min⁡∑i=1d𝜽′∈ℝd⁡pi​(ℓ⁡(𝜽′,𝒆i)+θi)−θk.\displaystyle=\max_{{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d}}\min_{\bm{\theta}^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}p_{i}(\ell(\bm{\theta}^{\prime};\bm{e}_{i})+\theta_{i})-\theta_{k}. (141)

By weak duality, we have for every (possibly non-convex) ℓ\ell

L−𝖧ℓ​(𝜽,𝒆k)\displaystyle L_{-\mathsf{H}_{\ell}}(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{k}) ≤min𝜽′∈ℝd⁡max⁡∑i=1d𝒑∈△d⁡pi​(ℓ⁡(𝜽′,𝒆i)+θi)−θk\displaystyle\leq\min_{\bm{\theta}^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\max_{{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}p_{i}(\ell(\bm{\theta}^{\prime};\bm{e}_{i})+\theta_{i})-\theta_{k} (142)
=min𝜽′∈ℝd⁡maxi∈[d]⁡ℓ⁡(𝜽′,𝒆i)+θi−θk.\displaystyle=\min_{\bm{\theta}^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\max_{i\in[d]}\ell(\bm{\theta}^{\prime};\bm{e}_{i})+\theta_{i}-\theta_{k}. (143)

We can see (𝜽;𝒆k)↦maxi∈[d]⁡ℓ⁡(𝜽′,𝒆i)+θi−θk(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{k})\mapsto\max_{i\in[d]}\ell(\bm{\theta}^{\prime};\bm{e}_{i})+\theta_{i}-\theta_{k} as a family of cost-augmented hinge losses (Tsochantaridis et al., 2005) parametrized by 𝜽′\bm{\theta}^{\prime}. Hence, L−𝖧ℓ​(𝜽,𝒆k)L_{-\mathsf{H}_{\ell}}(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{k}) is upper-bounded by the tightest loss in this family.

If ℓ\ell is convex, strong duality holds and we obtain equality

L−𝖧ℓ​(𝜽,𝒆k)=min𝜽′∈ℝd⁡maxi∈[d]⁡ℓ⁡(𝜽′,𝒆i)+θi−θk.\displaystyle L_{-\mathsf{H}_{\ell}}(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{k})=\min_{\bm{\theta}^{\prime}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}}\max_{i\in[d]}\ell(\bm{\theta}^{\prime};\bm{e}_{i})+\theta_{i}-\theta_{k}. (144)

Margin.

We can easily upper-bound the margin of L−𝖧ℓL_{-\mathsf{H}_{\ell}}. Indeed, assuming ℓ⁡(𝜽,𝒆i)\ell(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{i}) is upper-bounded by mm for all 𝜽\bm{\theta} and i∈[d]i\in[d], we get

0≤L−𝖧ℓ​(𝜽,𝒆k)≤maxi∈[d]⁡ℓ⁡(𝜽,𝒆i)+θi−θk≤maxi∈[d]⁡m+θi−θk.0\leq L_{-\mathsf{H}_{\ell}}(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{k})\leq\max_{i\in[d]}\ell(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{i})+\theta_{i}-\theta_{k}\leq\max_{i\in[d]}m+\theta_{i}-\theta_{k}. (145)

Hence, from Definition 8, we have margin⁡(L−𝖧ℓ)≤m\mathrm{margin}(L_{-\mathsf{H}_{\ell}})\leq m. Note that if margin⁡(L−𝖧ℓ)≤margin⁡(ℓ)\mathrm{margin}(L_{-\mathsf{H}_{\ell}})\leq\mathrm{margin}(\ell), then L−𝖧ℓ​(𝜽,𝒆k)=0⇒ℓ⁡(𝜽,𝒆k)=0L_{-\mathsf{H}_{\ell}}(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{k})=0\Rightarrow\ell(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{k})=0.

𝒑∈△d,𝝂\displaystyle{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d},\,\,\bm{\nu} ≥0.\displaystyle\geq 0. (177)

Let us define

τmin≔max⁡(𝜽)−g′​(1)andτmax≔max⁡(𝜽)−g′​(1d).\tau_{\min}\coloneqq\max(\bm{\theta})-g^{\prime}(1)\quad\text{and}\quad\tau_{\max}\coloneqq\max(\bm{\theta})-g^{\prime}\left(\frac{1}{d}\right).

Since gg is strictly convex, g′g^{\prime} is increasing and so τmin<τmax\tau_{\min}<\tau_{\max}. For any τ∈[τmin,τmax]\tau\in[\tau_{\min},\tau_{\max}], we construct 𝝂\bm{\nu} as

νj≔{0,θj−τ≥g′​(0)g′​(0)−θj+τ,θj−τ<g′​(0)\nu_{j}\coloneqq\begin{cases}0,&\theta_{j}-\tau\geq g^{\prime}(0)\\ g^{\prime}(0)-\theta_{j}+\tau,&\theta_{j}-\tau<g^{\prime}(0)\\ \end{cases}

By construction, νj≥0\nu_{j}\geq 0, satisfying dual feasibility. Injecting ν\nu into (175) and combining the two cases, we obtain

g′​(pj)=max⁡{θj−τ,g′​(0)}.g^{\prime}(p_{j})=\max\{\theta_{j}-\tau,~g^{\prime}(0)\}. (178)

We show that i) the stationarity conditions have a unique solution given τ\tau, and ii) [τmin,τmax][\tau_{\min},\tau_{\max}] forms a sign-changing bracketing interval, and thus contains τ⋆\tau^{\star}, which can then be found by one-dimensional search. The solution verifies all KKT conditions, thus is globally optimal.

Solving the stationarity conditions.

Since gg is strictly convex, its derivative g′g^{\prime} is continuous and strictly increasing, and is thus a one-to-one mapping between [0,1][0,1] and [g′​(0),g′​(1)][g^{\prime}(0),g^{\prime}(1)]. Denote by (g′)−1:[g′​(0),g′​(1)]→[0,1](g^{\prime})^{-1}\colon[g^{\prime}(0),g^{\prime}(1)]\rightarrow[0,1] its inverse. If θj−τ≥g′​(0)\theta_{j}-\tau\geq g^{\prime}(0), we have

g′​(0)≤g′​(pj)=θj−τ\displaystyle g^{\prime}(0)\leq g^{\prime}(p_{j})=\theta_{j}-\tau ≤max⁡(𝜽)−τmin\displaystyle\leq\max(\bm{\theta})-\tau_{\min} (179)
=max⁡(𝜽)−max⁡(𝜽)+g′​(1)\displaystyle=\max(\bm{\theta})-\max(\bm{\theta})+g^{\prime}(1)
=g′​(1).\displaystyle=g^{\prime}(1).

Otherwise, g′​(pj)=g′​(0)g^{\prime}(p_{j})=g^{\prime}(0). This verifies that the r.h.s. of (178) is always within the domain of (g′)−1(g^{\prime})^{-1}. We can thus apply the inverse to both sides to solve for pjp_{j}, obtaining

pj​(τ)=(g′)−1​(max⁡{θj−τ,g′​(0)}).p_{j}(\tau)=(g^{\prime})^{-1}(\max\{\theta_{j}-\tau,~g^{\prime}(0)\}). (180)

Strict convexity implies the optimal 𝒑⋆{\bm{p}}^{\star} is unique; it can be seen that τ⋆\tau^{\star} is also unique. Indeed, assume optimal τ1⋆,τ2⋆\tau^{\star}_{1},\tau^{\star}_{2}. Then, 𝒑⁡(τ1⋆)=𝒑⁡(τ2⋆){\bm{p}}(\tau^{\star}_{1})={\bm{p}}(\tau^{\star}_{2}), so max⁡(𝜽−τ1⋆,g′​(0))=max⁡(𝜽−τ2⋆,g′​(0))\max(\bm{\theta}-\tau^{\star}_{1},g^{\prime}(0))=\max(\bm{\theta}-\tau^{\star}_{2},g^{\prime}(0)). This implies either τ1⋆=τ2⋆\tau^{\star}_{1}=\tau^{\star}_{2}, or 𝜽−τ{1,2}⋆≤g′​(0)\bm{\theta}-\tau^{\star}_{\{1,2\}}\leq g^{\prime}(0), in which case 𝒑=𝟎∉△d{\bm{p}}=\bm{0}\notin\triangle^{d}, which is a contradiction.

Validating the bracketing interval.

Consider the primal infeasibility function ϕ⁡(τ)≔⟨𝒑⁡(τ),𝟏⟩−1\phi(\tau)\coloneqq{\langle{\bm{p}}(\tau),\bm{1}\rangle}-1; 𝒑⁡(τ){\bm{p}}(\tau) is primal feasible iff ϕ⁡(τ)=0.\phi(\tau)=0. We show that ϕ\phi is decreasing on [τmin,τmax][\tau_{\min},\tau_{\max}], and that it has opposite signs at the two extremities. From the intermediate value theorem, the unique root τ⋆\tau^{\star} must satisfy τ⋆∈[τmin,τmax]\tau^{\star}\in[\tau_{\min},\tau_{\max}].

Since g′g^{\prime} is increasing, so is (g′)−1(g^{\prime})^{-1}. Therefore, for all jj, pj​(τ)p_{j}(\tau) is decreasing, and so is the sum ϕ⁡(τ)=∑jpj​(τ)−1\phi(\tau)=\sum_{j}p_{j}(\tau)-1. It remains to check the signs at the boundaries.

∑ipi​(τmax)\displaystyle\sum_{i}p_{i}(\tau_{\max}) =∑i(g′)−1​(max⁡{θi−max⁡(𝜽)+g′​(1/d),g′​(0)})\displaystyle=\sum_{i}(g^{\prime})^{-1}(\max\{\theta_{i}-\max(\bm{\theta})+g^{\prime}\left(\nicefrac{{1}}{{d}}\right),~g^{\prime}(0)\}) (181)
≤d​(g′)−1​(max⁡{g′​(1/d),g′​(0)})\displaystyle\leq d~(g^{\prime})^{-1}(\max\{g^{\prime}\left(\nicefrac{{1}}{{d}}\right),~g^{\prime}(0)\})
=d​(g′)−1​(g′​(1/d))=1,\displaystyle=d~(g^{\prime})^{-1}\left(g^{\prime}\left(\nicefrac{{1}}{{d}}\right)\right)=1,

where we upper-bounded each term of the sum by the largest one. At the other end,

∑ipi​(τmin)\displaystyle\sum_{i}p_{i}(\tau_{\min}) =∑i(g′)−1​(max⁡{θi−max⁡(𝜽)+g′​(1),g′​(0)})\displaystyle=\sum_{i}(g^{\prime})^{-1}(\max\{\theta_{i}-\max(\bm{\theta})+g^{\prime}(1),~g^{\prime}(0)\}) (182)
≥(g′)−1​(max⁡{g′​(1),g′​(0)})\displaystyle\geq(g^{\prime})^{-1}(\max\{g^{\prime}(1),~g^{\prime}(0)\})
=(g′)−1​(g′​(1))=1,\displaystyle=(g^{\prime})^{-1}(g^{\prime}(1))=1,

using that a sum of non-negative terms is no less than its largest term. Therefore, ϕ⁡(τmin)≥0\phi(\tau_{\min})\geq 0 and ϕ⁡(τmax)≤0\phi(\tau_{\max})\leq 0. This implies that there must exist τ⋆\tau^{\star} in [τmin,τmax][\tau_{\min},\tau_{\max}] satisfying ϕ⁡(τ⋆)=0\phi(\tau^{\star})=0. The corresponding triplet (𝒑⁡(τ⋆),𝝂⁡(τ⋆),τ⋆)\left({\bm{p}}(\tau^{\star}),\bm{\nu}(\tau^{\star}),\tau^{\star}\right) thus satisfies all of the KKT conditions, confirming that it is the global solution.

Algorithm 1 is an example of a bisection algorithm for finding an approximate solution; more advanced root finding methods can also be used. We note that the resulting algorithm resembles the method provided in Krichene et al. (2015), with a non-trivial difference being the order of the thresholding and (−g)−1(-g)^{-1} in Eq. (180).

B.9 Proof of Proposition 15

We first need the following lemma.

Lemma 18.

Let ℓ⁡(𝛉,𝐞k)\ell(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{k}) be defined as

ℓ⁡(𝜽,𝒆k)≔{∑jck,j​ϕ​(θj) if ​𝜽⊤​𝟏=0∞ o.w. ,\ell(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{k})\coloneqq\begin{cases}\sum_{j}c_{k,j}\phi(\theta_{j})&\mbox{ if }\bm{\theta}^{\top}\bm{1}=0\\ \infty&\mbox{ o.w. }\end{cases}, (183)

where ϕ:ℝ→ℝ+\phi\colon{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}}_{+} is convex. Then, 𝖧ℓ\mathsf{H}_{\ell} defined in (138) equals

−𝖧ℓ​(𝒑)=min⁡∑jτ∈ℝ⁡(𝒑⊤​𝒄j)​ϕ∗​(−τ𝒑⊤​𝒄j).-\mathsf{H}_{\ell}({\bm{p}})=\min_{\tau\in{\mathbb{R}}}\sum_{j}({\bm{p}}^{\top}\bm{c}_{j})\phi^{*}\left(\frac{-\tau}{{\bm{p}}^{\top}\bm{c}_{j}}\right). (184)
Proof.

We want to solve

𝖧ℓ​(𝒑)=min⁡∑j𝜽⊤​𝟏=0⁡pj​ℓ​(𝜽,𝒆j)=min⁡∑j𝜽⊤​𝟏=0⁡pj​∑icj,i​ϕ​(θi)=min⁡∑i𝜽⊤​𝟏=0⁡(𝒑⊤​𝒄i)​ϕ​(θi),\mathsf{H}_{\ell}({\bm{p}})=\min_{\bm{\theta}^{\top}\bm{1}=0}\sum_{j}p_{j}\ell(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{j})=\min_{\bm{\theta}^{\top}\bm{1}=0}\sum_{j}p_{j}\sum_{i}c_{j,i}\phi(\theta_{i})=\min_{\bm{\theta}^{\top}\bm{1}=0}\sum_{i}({\bm{p}}^{\top}\bm{c}_{i})\phi(\theta_{i}), (185)

where 𝒄i\bm{c}_{i} is a vector gathering cj,ic_{j,i} for all jj. Introducing a Lagrange multiplier we get

𝖧ℓ​(𝒑)=min𝜽∈ℝ|𝒴|⁡max⁡∑iτ∈ℝ⁡(𝒑⊤​𝒄i)​ϕ​(θi)+τ​∑iθi.\mathsf{H}_{\ell}({\bm{p}})=\min_{\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{|{\mathcal{Y}}|}}\max_{\tau\in{\mathbb{R}}}\sum_{i}({\bm{p}}^{\top}\bm{c}_{i})\phi(\theta_{i})+\tau\sum_{i}\theta_{i}. (186)

Strong duality holds and we can swap the order of the min and max. After routine calculations, we obtain

−𝖧ℓ​(𝒑)=min⁡∑iτ∈ℝ⁡(𝒑⊤​𝒄i)​ϕ∗​(−τ𝒑⊤​𝒄i).-\mathsf{H}_{\ell}({\bm{p}})=\min_{\tau\in{\mathbb{R}}}\sum_{i}({\bm{p}}^{\top}\bm{c}_{i})\phi^{*}\left(\frac{-\tau}{{\bm{p}}^{\top}\bm{c}_{i}}\right). (187)

∎

We now prove Proposition 15. First, we rewrite ℓ⁡(𝜽,𝒆k)=∑j≠kϕ⁡(θj−θk)\ell(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{k})=\sum_{j\neq k}\phi(\theta_{j}-\theta_{k}) as ℓ⁡(𝜽,𝒆k)=∑jck,j​ϕ​(θj−θk)\ell(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{k})=\sum_{j}c_{k,j}\phi(\theta_{j}-\theta_{k}), where we choose ck,j=0c_{k,j}=0 if k=jk=j, 11 otherwise, leading to 𝒑⊤​𝒄j=1−pj{\bm{p}}^{\top}\bm{c}_{j}=1-p_{j}. Because ϕ⁡(θj−θk)\phi(\theta_{j}-\theta_{k}) is shift invariant w.r.t. 𝜽\bm{\theta}, without loss of generality, we can further rewrite the loss as ℓ⁡(𝜽,𝒆k)=∑jck,j​ϕ​(θj)\ell(\bm{\theta};\bm{e}_{k})=\sum_{j}c_{k,j}\phi(\theta_{j}) with 𝖽𝗈𝗆(ℓ)={𝜽∈ℝ|𝒴|:𝜽⊤​𝟏=0}\dom(\ell)=\{\bm{\theta}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{|{\mathcal{Y}}|}\colon\bm{\theta}^{\top}\bm{1}=0\}. Hence, Lemma 184 applies. We now derive closed form for specific choices of ϕ\phi.

Hinge loss.

When ϕ⁡(t)=[1+t]+\phi(t)=[1+t]_{+}, the conjugate is

ϕ∗​(u)={−u if ​u∈[0,1]∞ o.w. .\phi^{*}(u)=\begin{cases}-u&\mbox{ if }u\in[0,1]\\ \infty&\mbox{ o.w. }\end{cases}. (188)

The constraint set for τ\tau is therefore 𝒞≔⋂j∈[d][−𝒑⊤​𝒄j,0]=[−minj∈[d]⁡𝒑⊤​𝒄j,0]{\mathcal{C}}\coloneqq\bigcap_{j\in[d]}\left[-{\bm{p}}^{\top}\bm{c}_{j},0\right]=\left[-\displaystyle{\min_{j\in[d]}}~{\bm{p}}^{\top}\bm{c}_{j},0\right]. Hence

−𝖧ℓ​(𝒑)=minτ∈𝒞⁡d​τ=−d​minj∈[d]​𝒑⊤​𝒄j.-\mathsf{H}_{\ell}({\bm{p}})=\min_{\tau\in{\mathcal{C}}}d\tau=-d\min_{j\in[d]}{\bm{p}}^{\top}\bm{c}_{j}. (189)

This recovers Duchi et al. (2018, Example 5, §A.6) with a simpler proof. We next turn to the following new results.

Smoothed hinge loss.

We add quadratic regularization to the conjugate (Shalev-Shwartz and Zhang, 2016):

ϕ∗​(u)={−u+12​u2 if ​u∈[0,1]∞ o.w. .\phi^{*}(u)=\begin{cases}-u+\frac{1}{2}u^{2}&\mbox{ if }u\in[0,1]\\ \infty&\mbox{ o.w. }\end{cases}. (190)

Going back to ϕ\phi, we obtain:

ϕ⁡(t)={0 if ​t≤−1t+12 if ​t≥012​(1+t)2 o.w. .\phi(t)=\begin{cases}0&\mbox{ if }t\leq-1\\ t+\frac{1}{2}&\mbox{ if }t\geq 0\\ \frac{1}{2}(1+t)^{2}&\mbox{ o.w. }\end{cases}. (191)

The constraint set for τ\tau is the same as before, 𝒞=[−minj∈[d]⁡𝒑⊤​𝒄j,0]{\mathcal{C}}=\left[-\displaystyle{\min_{j\in[d]}}~{\bm{p}}^{\top}\bm{c}_{j},0\right].

Plugging ϕ∗\phi^{*} into (187), we obtain

−𝖧ℓ​(𝒑)=minτ∈𝒞⁡τ22​∑j=1d1𝒑⊤​𝒄j+d​τ.-\mathsf{H}_{\ell}({\bm{p}})=\min_{\tau\in{\mathcal{C}}}\frac{\tau^{2}}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\frac{1}{{\bm{p}}^{\top}\bm{c}_{j}}+d~\tau. (192)

Since the problem is unidimensional, let us solve for τ\tau unconstrained first:

τ=−d/(∑j=1d1/(𝒑⊤𝒄j)).\tau=-d\Big/(\sum_{j=1}^{d}1/({\bm{p}}^{\top}\bm{c}_{j})). (193)

We notice that τ≤−minj⁡𝒑⊤​𝒄j\tau\leq-\min_{j}{\bm{p}}^{\top}\bm{c}_{j} for 𝒄j≥𝟎\bm{c}_{j}\geq\bm{0} since ∑jmini⁡𝒑⊤​𝒄i𝒑⊤​𝒄j∈[0,d]\sum_{j}\frac{\min_{i}{\bm{p}}^{\top}\bm{c}_{i}}{{\bm{p}}^{\top}\bm{c}_{j}}\in[0,d]. This expression of τ\tau is not feasible. Hence the optimal solution is at the boundary and τ⋆=−minj⁡𝒑⊤​𝒄j\tau^{\star}=-\min_{j}{\bm{p}}^{\top}\bm{c}_{j}. Plugging that expression back into (192) gives the claimed expression of 𝖧ℓ\mathsf{H}_{\ell}.

Squared hinge loss.

When ϕ⁡(t)=12​[1+t]+2\phi(t)=\frac{1}{2}[1+t]^{2}_{+}, the conjugate is

ϕ∗​(u)={−u+12​u2 if ​u≥0∞ o.w. .\phi^{*}(u)=\begin{cases}-u+\frac{1}{2}u^{2}&\mbox{ if }u\geq 0\\ \infty&\mbox{ o.w. }\end{cases}. (194)

The constraint is now τ≤0\tau\leq 0. Hence, the optimal solution of the problem w.r.t. τ\tau in (187) is now (193) for all 𝒑∈△d,𝒄j≥𝟎{\bm{p}}\in\triangle^{d},\bm{c}_{j}\geq\bm{0}. Simplifying, we get

𝖧ℓ​(𝒑)=12​d2∑j=1d1/(𝒑⊤​𝒄j).\mathsf{H}_{\ell}({\bm{p}})=\frac{\frac{1}{2}d^{2}}{\sum_{j=1}^{d}1/({\bm{p}}^{\top}\bm{c}_{j})}. (195)

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
